inline.s: Reply to Magistrate Wang Dongli

Since we parted, I often feel as though we were still talking together on a frosty night under the moon. That scene, that hour, all lie within a dream; who among us can truly awake? To sit with a man beyond the world, a bowl of tea and a censer of incense between us, speaking of the unborn, is my constant thought. You write that of late you have read the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra and found places where your mind meets it; I am delighted. This sūtra is free from the marks of words and free from the marks of mental activity; only when one forgets words and subtly accords with it is there a way in. Once you no longer doubt, you will surely attain deep realization. Your further remark that a single illumination brings awakening, and that one can also turn circumstances around, is so; but to speak of “beating into one piece” is still to be separated by an iron mountain. This you must come to know yourself. If it does not become one piece, where is the fault? The ancients’ saying about becoming one piece is no small matter. From the first stirring of the resolve to investigate Chan, one takes a single kōan as the huatou, such as Zhaozhou’s “A dog has no Buddha-nature,” or “All dharmas return to the one; where does the one return?” and so on. Keep such a phrase across your chest, block off the root of the intellect, and never let it pass; raise a solid mass of doubt, clench your teeth day and night, and do not let a single thought go. Only after long practice does it become pure and ripe, and only then does it become one piece. In movement this takes ten or five years. This is the huatou becoming one piece; it is not yet realization becoming one piece. I know that you truly believe in this matter and already have places of understanding; but you have not yet put in the deadly effort the ancients did with the huatou. Even though one understands the principle, one is still at the gateway of lights and shadows; the mind of birth and death has not yet rested for a single thought. Thus in leisure, when nothing happens, there seems to be a principle; but when faced with circumstances and conditions, one is swept away. Know then that this matter cannot be turned to real use by understanding and principle. You also say that one should contemplate a single united mark, using seeing to break seeing, using marks to leave marks, using consciousness to remove consciousness, using attachment to break attachment. There is reason in this. But the single united mark is not something to be entered by bringing two ends together: it is precisely when mind and object are both forgotten that one has awakened to the one piece. When not the least dharma remains to obstruct the mind, when each thing dissolves and each dharma stands revealed — only thus may one enter the single united mark. If now you use seeing and knowledge to break it, it is like pouring oil into flour — how could it break anything? Moreover, seeing and knowledge are the very root of the disease, not a weapon against the enemy. To contemplate in this way seems to be muddled. If you enter by way of the teachings, you must follow the six metaphors of the Diamond Sutra; when that single contemplation is ripe, you will of itself be wholly in accord. If you enter by way of the Laṅkāvatāra, then simply in sitting quietly, being able to see the flow of your own mind’s delusive thoughts — that is where the work begins. You also say that in the phrase “delusive thoughts have no nature” you find strength, and so thought after thought dissolves. If you investigate within the school of Chan, simply follow the Sixth Patriarch’s “Not thinking good, not thinking evil — at that moment, what is the Venerable One’s original face?” This is the most direct and true. Work at it through the day without forgetting it, and do not seek the single united mark; when a single thought suddenly accords, you will suddenly fall into the one. I only hope that you will not seek the single united mark, nor fear being turned by circumstances, but simply carry one huatou with you always, and in daily life watch only where a single thought arises and bite it off on the spot — then it dissolves. If delusive thoughts dissolve, you will not be turned by any circumstance. If the eight consciousnesses burst open and you are thoroughly penetrated once and for all, then there is no circumstance to turn. When no circumstance can turn you, mind and circumstance are one — this is the true single united mark.

On my journey east I had the good fortune to meet you, a true man of the Way; the trip was not made in vain. This mountain rustic, in his old age, rests among green hills and white clouds, daily further from the world. Your vow to benefit living beings is flourishing; there will be no day for us to speak face to face. I am glad that your zeal in advancing on the Way is keen — truly a thousand li a day. Yet while swift progress in cultivation is easy, forgetting merit and cutting off realization is hard: clinging to the mysterious and dwelling in stillness, one sinks into a pit, and in time falls unwittingly into the demon’s net of views and knowledge. This is the one hard pass through which students of the Way since ancient times have struggled. Pass through it, and you take one more step from the top of a hundred-foot pole; arriving here, all is plain and ordinary, with nothing extraordinary left — the man is still the same as before, only his footing is no longer the old one. Then every pore of the body radiates light; this is decisively no realm of thought, decisively not sitting at the gate of lights and shadows. Here what matters is only to sweep away, step by step; thus you will naturally reach the great rest.

I have received your letter, and am humbled by your unflagging affection in the Dharma. Our minds meet and understand without the least separation; within the treasury of light we were never separable by bodily form — this is no empty saying. As to your account of your recent practice, day by day it grows more level and smooth; you have already trodden the ground of ease and joy, which fully proves the strength of your great diligence. When you say that the old nostril cannot bear the least thing clinging to it, that is precisely where the strength lies. But within that “cannot bear the least thing clinging,” there is still something muddled; you must see straight through it. The ancients said, “Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, hurry past.” They feared precisely that one might sit down inside the armor of nothing-to-do. If you do not see through this, the next turning will be even harder. Have you not heard Yunmen: there are two kinds of light that are not thoroughly penetrated. Not being clear in every place, with something present before you — that is one. Penetrating all dharmas as empty, yet seeming vaguely to have something there — that too is light not penetrated. The dharmakāya likewise has two illnesses. Having arrived at the dharmakāya’s side but not forgetting attachment to dharmas, with one’s own views still present — that is one. Even if you penetrate through, letting it go is still not permitted. Examine it finely: whatever breath or trace remains is likewise an illness. The ancients at first found seeing the Way hard; once the Way is seen, attachment to dharmas is hardest to dispel, and most fall here. As it is said, “To recognize it is still not to have it.” In this work there is no place to set your keenness, yet the one move of relinquishing dharma-views must not go unknown. What does your discernment make of this? In the past, relinquish thought after thought, until there is nothing left to relinquish; and do not sit down at the edge of nothing-left-to-relinquish either. Then you will naturally not be bound by views, and the whole body will be a great mass of fire.
To Bao Zhongsu, Director of the Ministry of Rites

Huangshan and the White Peak have long lain in the primordial vastness. By what karmic affinity has the spirit of the mountains shown its auspicious signs, moving the great protector of the Dharma, so that grey cliffs and emerald walls suddenly conjure up Brahma palaces and pearl-girt halls, and golden, wondrous images come forth from empty space, while the true words on palm leaves descend from heaven? In an instant a land without Buddha has welled up with the adornments of the Huayan store, drawing and transforming immeasurable gods and men to enter together the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Such wondrous function flows entirely from the single true mind of your compassionate thought; how could its merit and benefit be small? This mountain rustic reverently hears of it and praises it across the empty sky, regretting only that, old and frail, he cannot bow before it once. Lately I have chosen a valley on Mount Lu to pass my remaining years; fortunately Chen Chishi has become the temple’s benefactor, and we shall invite worthy men from within the seas to re-carve the Lotus water-clock. His letter says that you, Elder, have been the first to raise the call for a Jetavana. When I think how Mount Lu’s fame, applauded by worthy men, will lend glory to its cliffs and valleys — yet this rustic is unworthy of Master Yuan, and unfit to preside over the Donglin community.

At the New Year your messenger came from afar, and I was humbled by your unflagging kindness in wishing this mountain monk to make the journey, so as to form a bond of Dharma-joy. At first my heart was glad, and I set it all out before. Lately I received a letter from Sima Wang saying that the alarm in Liaodong is grave: on the twentieth day of the second month our troops marched, and of the four grand generals three have already fallen; eight or nine myriad living souls were in one morning ground to powder — enough to chill the heart. Only General Li’s single column remains; Liaodong is extremely hard to hold, and I fear a long drive southward — a great cause for anxiety. The court is in confusion, with no unified policy; conscription and grain transport are urgent as sparks and fire. What time is this? We disciples depend on the mountains and forests for such peace as we have. Thinking that men’s minds are now in turmoil, there is no leisure even to hide our traces and pour out our sincerity in prayer — how would I dare lightly go wandering for pleasure? That is the first reason. Further, I hear the capital is shaken, and that both north and south have banned monks, so that those who live by wandering have nowhere to set foot. If they heard where this rustic was, they would rush to him at the news; that they would not come is hard to guarantee, and I fear it would be inconvenient for the locality. That is the second reason. At first I thought the journey a pleasure; later one matter gave me cause for concern, and so I dared not lightly set out. I send this specially, and beg your compassionate understanding: let it be put off a while, and wait for a later time.

You have told me of your recent practice, and that you have gradually found a way in at the ground of your own mind; you wish for a secret phrase to serve as a shortcut. Now this matter is from the outset neither secret nor not-secret; it is done only at the single thought of the person concerned. Even the one move of looking into a huatou is a device used only because there is no alternative. What matters is to see through the mind of knowing and perceiving that appears before you in daily life: it is entirely the working of delusive thought. Even if there are profound and mysterious views and understandings, they are all shadows of the consciousness-spirit, all matters on the side of mind, intellect, and consciousness. In short, you have never understood the one move of transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness; therefore every stirring of mind and movement of thought falls into the pit of delusive thought. Hence the Buddha said, “All living beings, because they do not know the permanent abiding true mind, employ all manner of delusive thoughts; these thoughts are not real, and so there is turning about.” This is what Aśvaghoṣa meant in saying that all living beings, from the beginning, have never been apart from thought. Know then that the many delusive thoughts of living beings in daily life are, in the end, only this one delusive thought. And this one thought is precisely the first source from which confusion arose; from beginningless time until now there has been only this one thought, and no second. Mind, intellect, and consciousness all arise upon this one thought. If in your practice you can see through this one thought, then all delusive thoughts and emotional calculations will at once be clear as ice. This is what is meant by “one who is free from the mark of thought is equal to the realm of space.” Yet living beings see only the delusive thoughts in their minds, teeming and jostling, so many of them, and in truth do not know that they are only one thought. Since they cannot in fact separate themselves from that tangle of thoughts, the ancients taught people to raise a huatou as their practice. Investigate it: the huatou too is a delusive thought. It is simply used to dam up scattered thoughts and gather them into one. If you probe this one thought deeply, look and look again, you will find that it originally has no place of arising; it is by nature unborn. Once you awaken to the un-bornness of this one thought, the roots of conditioning from countless kalpas will be shed on the spot. This is called awakening; it is not that there is some other mystery to be awakened to. Now as for you, old layman, in raising the huatou, apply your effort only to this one thought; probe it deeply, and suddenly you will see that this one thought has no place of birth. If you understand the un-bornness of one thought, then from that point on all thoughts are un-born. This is what the Sixth Patriarch called “dwelling nowhere, yet giving rise to mind.” If you seek the mysterious, then you are dwelling. This direct and immediate point is the most powerful; there is no need to seek much understanding. Not a single word applies here; you need only first lay down all the delusive thoughts and views in your breast, lay them down until the mind is empty and free, not a thread remaining. Then watch the place where a thought arises, and apply your effort there in probing it. This is a single blade driving straight in; it does not allow thinking ahead or reckoning behind, or any kind of calculation. The moment there is reckoning, you are far, far away. Since you have set your mind on this matter, old layman, try taking it up in this way.
Reply to Qian Shouzhi, Hanlin Academician

This mountain rustic is deeply ashamed to be a cracked vessel, a disgrace to the Dharma-gate; and further, having long been sunk in the miasmic seas, I was content to fill the ditches. I did not expect that Heaven would grant me remaining life, or that I should still be here today. Formerly, being old and often ill, I meant to hide my shadow in remote mountains; but just then there was an unfinished karmic bond at Shuangjing, one that touched life and death, so that I could not omit this one journey — hence I came stumbling along. Though I dare not speak of Sudhana’s pilgrimage south, I count it fortune to have visited teachers far and wide. I have long regarded you, layman, as a Pei Du or Yang Yi of our day and a bulwark of the Dharma-gate, and knowing your compassionate mindfulness to be earnest, I planned to call at your chamber. Yesterday I heard that your compassionate vessel had waited for me at Xishan, and that I missed you face to face; I was greatly dismayed. Then, humbled, I received your compassionate letter from afar, with all manner of Dharma offerings; I have held and recited it again and again, and my feelings grow only deeper, the more so as my delusive thoughts fly beyond measure. I can by no means delay. But the rain and snow are unbroken; I shall leave the mountains at the first clearing. I still have one journey to Yunqi, and shall not linger long by the lake. When I return by way of Wumen, I shall certainly enter the chamber of Vimalakīrti. I send this first to thank you; no more now.

In my ordinary dwelling this mountain rustic is constantly grieved at the decline of the Dharma-gate: even among outer protectors and guardians of the teaching, a man who truly bears the burden is hard to find. Yesterday I had the good fortune to meet you, layman, and my long-cherished hope was greatly comforted. Manifesting the body of a magistrate and raising the banner of the true Dharma — at such a time there is great promise in this. As for me, a withered stump, a discarded thing of the Dharma-gate, I am humbled by the depth of your Dharma-affection, and I trust in a karmic bond from former lives. At our meeting on Mount Yu we were hurried and could not fully set out what was in my heart; you humbled me further by escorting me far in a linked boat, and still more by your unflagging care. After we parted I reached Mount Kuang in the latter half of midsummer, and chose a dwelling south of the mountain among the Seven Worthies and Five Peaks, where I cut thatch for a few rafters and lodge as best I can. When I sent my few lines before, I had not yet settled on a resting place. All along old age and illness have assailed me; this phantom body suffers from a damp ailment, and only as winter came did I feel somewhat better. In compiling the Record of Dharma Protection, I read it against the records from time to time; the stupa inscriptions of the venerable ones point word by word to the one road above, and hold the true eye of the Chan school. In our Ming dynasty the Dharma-fortune has opened wide, and we rely on this as our mirror. If it is carved and circulated, the benefit to the Dharma will be no shallow thing. As for the manuscript, I shall bring it in person next spring.

I previously sent you my Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra; this sūtra is precisely the true artery of the Mind school. I do not know whether you have given it your attention. Of late, among the monks of the southeast, many investigate the one road above, but to their sorrow they have no clear-eyed master to instruct them; all fall to the gateway of lights and shadows, juggling the consciousness-spirit, and are ruined by the seal of the winter melon. Nor are they willing to draw near the teachings and seek true right views — truly a sad state. Among magistrates these thirty years there have been no few with the great resolve to protect the Dharma; yet those who truly settle their minds in the work of the original ground are likewise few. For the most part the scholar-officials are far too clever: whether it be Chan or the teachings, they take it all in with a single nod. From those who formerly enjoyed great reputations in men’s eyes, this can be generally seen. At this time, not only in worldly truth but even more within the Dharma-gate, things are harder still; to speak of it brings tears. Now, when the ways of the world are thin and the Dharma-gate is in decline, unless a person of great strength appears, who will uphold it? I have often said that to set the world right lies in rectifying men’s minds, and to protect the Dharma-gate lies in rectifying views and understanding. Yet to rectify men’s minds, one must take right views as the root. As it is said, “Unbiased and unpartisan, the kingly way is broad and level.” Without a mind utterly impartial and selfless, how could one unite the feelings of the multitude and settle the will of the crowd? Now the learning of selflessness must come from the work of investigation within the Dharma: one must thoroughly break apart body, mind, and world, and lay bare the treasury of great light that is originally possessed; only then can one regard body and world as a flower in the sky or a bubble’s shadow, and look on fame and rank as a dream, an illusion, water, or the moon. Then of oneself one equalizes life and death, makes right and wrong one, and rises above praise and blame. Only thus may one dare to speak of regarding the whole world as one family and all living beings as one body, magnanimous and greatly impartial. Then men’s minds are of themselves rectified, the ways of the world may become simple and honest, and the effect of aiding the ruler and benefiting the people surpasses all else. Examining closely the learning of Zhou Dunyi of the Song, it truly issued from this; hence he could serve as wings to the sage founder and open a work of ten thousand generations of peace. Reading the Record of Dharma Protection, I never fail to stroke the scroll and sigh. The customs of this decadent age are in great part beyond recovery; only such a man as this can speak of the governance of great peace. Moreover, the way of Heaven revolves without cease — how could this world be utterly without such a man? This mountain rustic is ashamed to be a discarded thing of the Dharma-gate, of no benefit to the world in his life; yet my heart of concern for the Dharma is as if it issued from my own person. Therefore what I hope for from you, layman, is weighty and great. I earnestly pray that you take the time to store up and nourish yourself deeply, so as to await Heaven’s favor. For the altars of state and the common people, my neck is stretched and I stand on tiptoe in the extreme. How could you bear not to bring forth a deep mind and a heavy vow? As for the Record of Dharma Protection, the essays need not be heavily annotated; simply set out one or two points where the stupa inscriptions of the patriarchs open the true eye — that will already be superfluous enough. I hope you will have it carved soon. Recently I composed my Comprehensive Discussion of the Śūraṅgama; I have already had it sent for your perusal. This sūtra is vast, containing the whole of the Buddha’s teaching for one generation: delusion and awakening, cause and effect — no principle is left unreached. Past interpreters have not fully drawn it out; my work departs greatly from the old ruts, and seems easier to enter. My Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus likewise overturns all the old verdicts. Without knowing the Lotus, one cannot know the Tathāgata’s bitter heart in saving the world; without knowing the Śūraṅgama, one cannot know the crucial point of cultivating the mind through delusion and awakening; without knowing the Laṅkāvatāra, one cannot distinguish right from wrong in views and understanding. These three sūtras, layman, you should investigate with a deep mind; another day I shall ask more of you.

The Record of Dharma Protection is nothing other than a transmission-lamp record of the Chan school. What it prizes is possession of the Dharma-eye of the school: it observes a man’s capacity and the relation of teacher and disciple, his gate of awakening, his conduct, his undertakings — and as for the final move, that above all is held great. Here it is written out whole from the tip of the brush; not only is the writing excellent, but in its deep heart of protecting the Dharma not a word fails to flow from actuality. As for the sources of the teaching and the transmission of the explicit and secret, it is exhaustive and leaves nothing out. This is a book of peerless song through the ages, not to be compared with others’ gleanings. For now I take only those among the stupa inscriptions of the great elders of the school that take right view and right conduct as their main point. Where your views, layman, largely agree, I do not presume to add further defilement. As for the stele records and prefaces, those are merely literature, and so are unnecessary. I am sending the base copy by the next post. If it is carved one day earlier, the Dharma-gate receives one day’s benefit the sooner. This mountain monk formerly read the collected works of the August Emperor Taizu: those relating to Buddhism, together with the prefaces to the various sūtras, and in the five temples built at Nanjing — Tianjie, Bao’en, Linggu, Nengren, and Jiming — each has its own imperial record; the important deeds recorded in those registers I have meant to gather into one book, so as to reveal the sage founder’s heart of protecting the Dharma. If it were made into one volume together with this record, it would show that in our illustrious dynasty the founding ruler and his ministers were of one body — something without parallel in past or present. I hope you, layman, will take note and make a search for these; it would be a most excellent undertaking, and truly what this mountain monk most desires.

I am humbled by your letter, which tells me in full of your recent circumstances, and further recounts the closing sentence in Meigong’s note — something this rustic has long held in his heart, and not only now. As for the retirement society, it began with the vow-power of the chief seat Huicheng; I praised it, and was willing simply to give up my dwelling — that is all. What time is this? There is no leisure even to seek safety; why should I make more trouble for myself? Moreover, in recent years decline and illness come daily; my feet suffer a damp ailment and walking is difficult. My mountain dwelling is rough, and I lodge there as best I can. I fear my remaining days are few, and my mind is urgent about birth and death; so I have closed the pass and cut off conditions, single-mindedly holding one thought, waiting for death — that is all. Last Mid-Autumn I had already begun. For twenty years and more I have thought of the winds and waves of the sea of suffering, of green hills and white clouds, and they have been with me even in dreams. Now that I have suddenly obtained this, would I be willing to regard it as a trifling thing? Now within the pass I bundle up all Chan talk and Buddhadharma and put it on a high shelf, and keep only to keeping my clumsiness. I often think how the ancients recited Amitābha’s name a hundred thousand times day and night; now I am ashamed that, old and with little strength of body, I can at my best manage barely half when I test myself. So I follow the example of Master Yuan and his six-period lotus water-clock, using incense in place of flowers, and for several months now body and mind have of themselves reached the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Knowing the depth of your concern, I have dared to tell you.

The attendant has returned and I have your Dharma-letter; I know that of late your mind-ground is free and untrammelled. This is not easy to obtain without true practice. I am greatly comforted, greatly comforted. You set out for me the essentials of the gate of non-duality: they surpass nothing of the High Seat’s one device, and it is not merely one dharma. The preface on the Mind-Dharma is truly a rash piece of talk; humbled by your great hand in correcting it, it has suddenly become fine writing — the work of an alchemist turning back the elixir. I dare not say it must be transmitted, but it preserves one kind of Dharma-gate, that is all. You note that the affairs of the realm are difficult and that none is willing to risk death’s utmost. This is true. Yet observe the men of old who gave their bodies for their country: it did not come from a momentary impulse. Such persons arise from many causes and conditions, and are not easily matched. First, when living beings face great calamity, there is of itself a kind of bodhisattva of great compassion who comes forth by vow; his workings are all issued from spiritual power, and do not come from delusive thought, calculation, or reckoning. This was so in the past; even the heroes of the time of our Sage Founder were such men. Second, there are those born in response to the times to uphold the world: inwardly endowed with the numinous root of prajñā, outwardly furnished with the tools of response, they possess the root beforehand, and when the moment comes their use is like reaching into a bag — a hundred shots, a hundred hits. The Marquis of Liu and Zhuge Liang, with the Lords of Pingyuan and Zhongding, were such men. Third, there are those who likewise come from the vow-power of prajñā, bearing the habit-energies of loyalty, righteousness, courage, and decisiveness from many lives, upright and impartial, firm beyond shaking; they settle great matters and hold fast without change. Wen Tianxiang and Fang Xiaoru of the Ming were such men — men whose native character is fixed beyond seizure. Now, among the figures in the world today, is there one such? Looking at their speech and discussion, is there one with a view firm enough to quell disorder and uphold what is falling? To demand actual results where the root is absent — is that not excessive? Hence the loyal ministers of old had settled talents and capacities, and tools with which they could surely accomplish; unused they remained at rest, but used they surely produced results. Even among those of the present age who combine both talents and tools, who is such a man? Therefore those of old who established unshakable merit had it all settled in their breasts beforehand, like Fan Li, Zifang, and the Lord of Wu; advancing and withdrawing, they had room to spare. How could they take empty talk for actual achievement? Even Su Dongpo was but a man of letters and integrity. Now you, layman, are one to whom the age looks; but consider for yourself your own tools — how do they compare with those lords? What you possess is but a single loyal heart. If talent and tools are not sufficient, how dare one speak of the great affairs of the world? This is what this rustic has earnestly hoped you would deeply cultivate. By my old eyes, considering your heart, layman, you can surely assess the undertakings those lords could accomplish, and your will can accomplish them. But as for quelling disorder and upholding what is falling — with what art would you do it? Could that be something forged on the spot? Even the matter now before us is a trifle; there are greater things than this. I only pray that you, layman, store up your tools early, and do not be so good as to hand over your very life — that is the complete strategy. The whole world is deluded; how could one shout awake the many? Knowing that you, layman, are of a mind to leave the mountains, I have sent this especially. I hope you will slow your advance, hold your tools, and wait for the time. Heaven must have its intent, and will bring great work to completion; by no means take it lightly. If your long nurture is already complete, come forth with the times and act at the first sight, like a grey hawk seizing a hare, leaving no trace of shadow — that is the bearing of a great hand. How could it be right to follow men for the sake of face and count the surrender of your life a gain? What does your discernment make of this?

Since receiving your letter of last autumn, when you left the mountains, in which you said that the nourishing of the body must wait its time, my humble heart has been greatly comforted. I did not expect that the fortunes of the realm would be so full of trouble — outer calamity and inner anxiety, court and countryside in fear, the young Sage standing alone, the heavy burden hard to bear. Fortunately a time of Kui and Long ministers, thronging and able; above, we rely on the spirits of our ancestors; below, we answer the hopes of the common people. You, layman, should firmly hold your vow-power, take up the bearing as your mind, and hold back the wild waves. By no means take generous passion for your task, nor find it hard to go up and down with the times as a skillful device. This vegetable-and-bamboo-shoot heart of the mountain forest will surely have its resting place within the treasury of great light. The wonder of the great Way, as it is said, is hard to convey in words. These years this rustic’s decline and illness grow daily; I do not think I shall long remain in the world, and in this life there will be no further meeting. To speak of it is bitter and sour. What this rustic grieves over is not the times alone: the Dharma-way is sparse indeed, and among those in my eyes on whom the heart of protection rests, such as you, layman, I can no longer count a second on my fingers — how much less a diamond banner! On my journey to Lingnan I gained one disciple who sealed the mind — a certain Feng Changli, one of the surviving writings of the Four Masters. A pity he died young. (Several lines are missing at the end of the letter.)
To Xu Qingzhi, Grand Secretary

You have told me in full of your recent circumstances, and my unflagging concern is deeply comforted. The Sage said, “Only when the year turns cold does one know the pine and cypress.” A great man in the world perfects his resolve through many hardships. Having passed through this trial, layman, your bones will be firm and your temper mild, your heart strong and your body sound, and so you will perfect the late discipline of blessing and long life. Thus those who hemmed you in were all Heaven’s way of forging you — all of them your good teachers. Seen so, there is cause for rejoicing and more; why should any grudge remain? It is said that among men there are things to be forgotten and things not to be forgotten: one who has shown me virtue must not be forgotten; one who has shown me resentment may be forgotten. Moreover, a man’s fortune and emolument are fixed to the last hair beforehand; their loss and gain lie not with others but are what I originally possess. After this you should hold firmly to the strength of the Way, keep far from unprofitable friends, cut down unprofitable expense, and whenever a thought arises, set your mind only on future blessing. That is truly a man of measureless greatness. What do you think, what do you think?
Reply to Duan Huanran, Supervising Secretary

I have received your letters one after another, and see fully your heart of anxiety for country and people, and for the Dharma-gate. And you have humbled me by asking this mountain monk’s thoughts — how deep your feeling is! This mountain monk, though a mere plant or tree of a man, has always cherished the vow to leave the world, to be a loyal minister of the Dharma-king and a filial son of the Compassionate Father. This is no empty talk; it has been tested. As for the teaching that the Buddha’s fixed karma must be accepted, I have known it for many years. Now, unhappily, in my declining years I see the world in disorder; this is a kalpa of calamity that all must meet — how could completed karma be escaped? Yet to seek escape and not find it is what is called fixed karma; if one could escape and does not, that is folly. And to hold stubbornly to folly, taking no account of the Dharma-gate — is that wisdom? Having repeatedly received your clear instruction, I deeply feel the abundant heart of one who protects the Dharma — and not for this mountain monk alone. Yet what you teach is that as soon as one hears of disorder, one should overturn the meditation platform, shout the assembly away, and withdraw oneself; that is panic and loss of composure, and seems not what a wise man should have. This mountain monk cannot do it: that is the first. You say that wandering alone with a single bowl is lofty and pure; but this mountain monk is nearly eighty, and unworthy beside Zhaozhou: that is the second thing I cannot do. You say that Qiuyue is a place to retire and support one’s old age, and that there one may hide one’s name; but I hear that Qiuyue’s mountain estate is several tens of li, abounding in fruit trees and things that sustain life — and I fear I would lack the strength to keep it, and would then have to hand it over to a prince’s household and beg protection from magistrates. If he is so fond of fame, is that a fit place to avoid fame? If I went, they would take me for rare merchandise to be traded — and an old cow will not be haltered: that is the fourth thing I cannot do. And to draw near a name in order to avoid a name, going where others go, is like the sacred turtle dragging its tail in the mud: that is the fifth thing I cannot do. Your love for me and anxiety for me, old layman, are indeed earnest and deep; but there are five reasons why this mountain monk cannot accept your instruction, and so I hesitate and cannot decide. You said before that Caoxi too cannot be a place to hide. Speaking by locality, it truly cannot be hidden; but judged by principle, this is something you, old layman, do not know. The reason you say it cannot be hidden is the worry over sea pirates. But Caoxi is nearly a thousand li from the sea, and sails do not reach it: that is the first freedom from care. The mountain is not deep, but the place lies in a quiet corner; even if the whole world were in disorder, it would not be worth contending for: that is the second. The monastery is now a thousand years old and has passed through many dynasties; the greatest disorder was the Five Dynasties of the Tang, and Huang Chao was the worst. Yet when his own troops came here, moved by the spirit of the Sixth Patriarch, he gave up his camp grounds as fields for the community’s support — to this day called Huang Chao’s estate. Thus a demon king became a protector of the Dharma: that is the third. Moreover the patriarch’s hall and the meditation hall are the monastery I myself raised; of all my life’s work only this one matter remains, and every part of it is what I originally possess. To go there is like going home, with no need to flee far to Zhongnan: that is the fourth. And the sons and grandsons of Caoxi are all disciples I have raised and nurtured; they now long for me as for a loving father, and if I go it will be as a father looking on his children, with no need to seek anyone’s favor: that is the fifth. As for support, it depends not only on former benefactors: the mountain fields here can be ploughed and vegetables and fruit eaten, with no need to seek far in the world or wait on others: that is the sixth. And the Sixth Patriarch’s remains of the Way are as if alive — the dharmakāya ever abiding; if I rely on this place, then I shall live with the dharmakāya as my life. If the dharmakāya were destroyed, living beings would die: that is the seventh. I have heard that the loyal give their bodies for their country; if one dies on the frontier, then death itself is imperishable. Now this mountain monk wishes to be a loyal minister of the Dharma-king and to hold the Buddha-patriarchs’ wisdom-life as weighty. If I am on Mount Kuang, that is truly not a place to retire, and even if I keep to fixed karma, my death would be of no benefit. If I am at Caoxi, then with one day’s leisure I can guide those who come to learn and continue the wisdom-life, so that the Buddhadharma is not cut off. There, even if I meet great disorder and fixed karma cannot be escaped, my death will be imperishable — just as one who gives his body for his country dies on the frontier, and so dies in the right place. Is that not fortunate? Moreover, there I avoid five cares and gain seven freedoms from care, and what I take up is what I originally possess. Why should I fear and not do it? The provincial authorities there have already three times sent letters, begging me to return to the mountain these three years. Now the prefect’s office has issued documents and sent monks to invite me, sitting here in wait. This mountain monk, unable to decline, will answer the summons and go. I truly fear that when you, old layman, hear of it, you will think I have disobeyed your great teaching; therefore I dare to set it all out one by one, to comfort your deep heart of Dharma-protection. By no means let rumors startle your hearing. Only let your mind understand it.
Reply to Prefect Yuan Cangru

Having repeatedly received your letters, I know that you have taken refuge in the Pure Land, decided beyond doubt. Where there is no doubt, there is decisive faith. Excellent, excellent. You also say that concerning the nearness or distance of Tianru’s Pure Land, the simile of imagining India remains unsettled. But that simile was never apt; the dream simile, which you then cite, is the most apt of all. Yet you still have not distinguished between the imagining of a pure land and of a defiled one, and so the meaning of “mind-only” is not clear to you. The Buddha said that all dharmas are like a dream or an illusion, and again that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like last night’s dream, and again that purity and defilement follow the mind, and again that by day it is the thinking mind and by night it takes form in dreams. So let me use the dream to explain the meaning of mind-only, and try to set it out. Now imagining may be defiled or pure, and both are roots of birth-and-death; hence it is said that all worlds are upheld by imagining alone. Chan practice requires one to be free of imagining, while the Pure Land requires single-minded imagining: this is using imagining to remove imagining, a method of exchange. Because living beings’ daily thoughts are defiled imaginings that only create the bitter karma of birth-and-death, one who now wishes to escape suffering thinks pure thoughts, thought after thought, imagining the Buddha and the Pure Land. When pure imagining prevails, defiled imagining fades; as it fades, pure imagining becomes pure; when it is pure, a defiled land is transformed into a pure land. A man who imagines lust will dream of sexual acts; though the acts are false, in the dream they are nonetheless taken as real. If a man by day thinks only of the Pure Land, then by night he will dream of terraces of transformation and jewelled ground, the realm of Ultimate Bliss, and enjoy it at ease — and that is a real thing. Thus the Pure Land lies only in the difference between dreaming and waking; how could it have a real nearness or distance? Therefore when the Buddha spoke of a mind-only Pure Land, he meant precisely what a single pure thought conjures and transforms. Hence it is said that when imagining is settled it becomes a land. Yet this Sahā world of defilement is entirely the congealed product of living beings’ defiled imaginings, wholly foul; while the Brahmā king Śikhin saw it as wholly pure. It is just like the Ganges: men see it as cool water, hungry ghosts see it as fire. Thus the followers of the two vehicles see Sahā as a defiled land and feel deep loathing, because they do not understand that the defiled is the pure. Hence at the assembly of the Lotus the Buddha three times transformed Sahā into a pure land, to point out that what lies before us in daily life, every step and every thing, is all the Pure Land. How then could there be a distance of a hundred thousand koṭis of lands? Yet when the sūtra speaks of a hundred thousand koṭis, the Buddha is pointing to the Huayan world: to the west of Sahā, past a hundred thousand koṭi buddha-lands, there is the Land of Ultimate Bliss — the land of actual reward where Amitābha Buddha dwells — so that people may know where to turn. If we speak of mind-only, then the Huayan world too is mind-only, and how much more the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Let me explain the meaning of mind-only by a nearby example. As a youth this rustic heard the Huayan Sūtra and, hearing of the ten-thousand-year ice and snow of Mount Wutai, earnestly wished to dwell on that mountain; day and night he thought of it. After a long time he saw before him only a snow mountain; walking, standing, sitting, and lying, he was always within it. Even passing through a crowded market, he saw not a single person, but walked only in the snow mountain. Later when he reached Wutai, it was exactly as he had imagined. From this one may know the nearness or distance of the Pure Land. Yet Wutai still required the body to arrive; the Pure Land requires only that the mind arrive. If one single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, thought after thought visualizing the Pure Land, then after a long time of ripening, in daily life, at every step and in everything, one will be as if sitting, lying, walking, and standing within the Pure Land. Then every sound the ear hears will be the sound of Buddha-recitation. Reciting thus until the end of life, all the world’s mixed thoughts will no longer appear, and only the single thought of Amitābha Buddha will remain. Then one will be diligent and undistracted; before one’s eyes will appear only the Pure Land, or a lotus flower, and Amitābha Buddha with the bodhisattvas will come in person to receive and guide one. The spirit will be at peace and will follow the Buddha straight to rebirth, and in that instant ascend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, no different from the dream before. How then could there be a distance of a hundred thousand koṭi of lands? This is what is meant by “rebirth is decisively attained, yet in going one truly does not go.” It is utterly true and actual, not a matter of discussing principles. One need only ripen single-minded pure imagining, and exchange it for defiled imagining; then of itself a defiled land becomes a pure land. As for the saying that rebirth in the Pure Land is like a dream — this is not a metaphor but the plain truth. In the bodhisattvas’ cultivation, even up to the seventh ground, none has yet broken the dream of ignorance; all their teaching and transforming of beings and perfecting of pure lands are buddha-work within a dream. Hence the bodhisattva of the eighth ground crosses the river as in a dream, not yet abiding in awakening; only at Buddhahood is one called greatly awakened. This is stated plainly and fully recorded in the Huayan Sūtra — clear evidence. Only past speakers have never taken it up. If you understand this, old layman, then all doubts about the nearness or distance of the Pure Land will be exhausted without remainder. As for the practice of Buddha-recitation, what the Amitābha Sūtra sets out is simply single-mindedness and undistraction; that is the definitive word. In truth even this word is not easy to reach. Test it in your own mind, old layman: whether rebirth in the Pure Land is certain or not can be seen only in whether a single thought is distracted. Then you will silently have faith, like a man drinking water knowing for himself, and of yourself you will be diligent. You write that you have long been in the Tiantai school, and now wish to harmonize the three contemplations of the Tiantai Pure Land. In this matter the Commentary on the Profound Meaning is the clearest. As the Tiantai house puts it, though the contemplations are sixteen, to speak of the Buddha encompasses them all; thus contemplation of the Buddha is the comprehensive contemplation. In this contemplation of the Buddha and recitation of the Buddha, the three contemplations are present within the recitation. It is said that precisely when one is contemplating and reciting the Buddha, one should lay down body and mind, inside and out, not keeping the least thing, so that the mind-ground is like space and not a single dharma is seen: this is the contemplation of emptiness. Then, within this empty mind, raise the sound of the Buddha; with the place where the thought is raised, contemplate the Buddha’s image, as if seeing it before one’s eyes, clear and unmistaken: this is the contemplation of the provisional. And while thus contemplating, turn the light back on the mind-essence that contemplates and recites, empty and still — and within that emptiness and stillness, again not forgetting the contemplation. Neither forgetting nor clinging, with the one mind luminous: this is the contemplation of the middle way. These three contemplations require no arranging; simply raise the thought, and the three contemplations are one mind, complete in a single thought. Nor should one here apply the three contemplations as once arranged, for to set the mind to it is not wondrous. Try applying your effort here.

I know, old layman, that you are setting to work on your own behalf, and that your resolve is most urgent; this is the thought that birth-and-death is a great matter, and now is the time of urgency. But as to the work of investigation, it has always been said that one raises a kōan or huatou; as Chan Master Dahui strongly maintained, all who awakened the mind in the Chan gate before him did so through the work of raising a huatou. Yet in the way they applied the mind there is much difference. To speak today of raising a huatou is even more mistaken; the application of mind is far off, because people know only how to raise it and do not know that letting go is the essential wonder. The ancients’ single move of letting go is the most essential word for entering the Way. Know then that the word “raise” means to raise precisely where one has let go, not merely to keep thinking of the huatou. Aśvaghoṣa said that the mind-essence is free of thought and equal to the realm of space, and again that the state of being free of thought is known only by realization. Since the mind-essence is originally free of thought, people today do not know that freedom from thought is right mindfulness, and so they cling to and raise a single mind, and thereby only increase their confusion. How is it that raising is done precisely where one has let go? Take Amitābha Buddha as the huatou: before raising the Buddha, one must first let go of outer objects, then let go of all the delusive thoughts of the inner mind, and then let go of this very thought of letting go. When there is nowhere left to let go, only then, from within this, apply your effort and raise the sound of the Buddha. Then watch this one sound of the Buddha: where does it come from, and where does it now fall to? Steady the diamond eye and fix it with a single look; look until there is no place for it to land, then again raise and again look, again pursue to the place where a single thought is unborn — and you will see the original face. At first one applies the mind to look and pursue; when the pursuit reaches the point where the single thought is cut off at both ends, the middle is of itself solitary. Then, from this solitary place, sharply gather your keenness and pursue straight on. Suddenly the mass of doubt bursts open, and the original face appears of itself. This then is the true un-bornness of a single thought. If a student can simply bring this single un-born thought before him, he will gain great use in every place; this is the season of escaping birth-and-death. In recent times people do not know to seek, at the place of letting go, the one move of freedom from thought; they cling rigidly to the huatou, and so add to their obstacles. What is more, they raise all sorts of thoughts and store up profound and mysterious views beforehand — this is the very root that obstructs the Way. Thus although your investigation, old layman, is earnest, you have not had the one move of letting go explained to you; you are obstructed only by the shadow of the habit-energy of the profound and mysterious, and so you gain no use from it. Among all the hundred thousand devices, none is more effort-saving than the one move of letting go. Do the work at this effortless place, and then thought after thought in daily life will be true and actual use. Let your discernment look into it.
To Yuan Gongliao

I have often said that the great and heroic men of old who could establish great merit and found great works all came through the endurance of insult. Even becoming a Buddha takes the practice of patience as foremost; hence the term “the patiently accepted un-bornness of dharmas.” Of all sages and worthies, none succeeded except through patience, and none failed except through impatience. As a youth this old fellow read the Records of the Historian, and when he came to the Lives of Han Xin and Zhang Liang he looked to see how such men, able to establish great works, had in the end come from where. Examining their conduct in detail, he came suddenly upon Han Xin in the Huaiyin marketplace, suffering the insult of crawling between a lout’s legs; Han Xin looked at him long, then went through. Here one may see in the historian’s single word “long” the whole learning of a lifetime written out. And at the bridge on the Yi, the shoe was brought three times, and only then did the old man approve. His iron hammer at Bolang was broken by a single straw sandal. Thus one knows where the ancients found their strength. All my life this old fellow has entered the Buddhadharma through this; hence what I wrote before — it is the crotch of the Huai marketplace and the shoe on the Yi bridge.
To Zhou Haimen, Chief Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud

Since we parted, twenty years have slipped by in a blink, and it is more than ten years since word has passed between us. Our spirits are surely not estranged, yet it is not as satisfying as receiving your countenance and hearing your voice. Last spring, at Yunqi, I meant to receive your teaching by the lake, and waited long without your coming; disappointed, I returned to the mountains. Heaven has lent this poor monk remaining life, and I may await death on Mount Kuang — a great fortune indeed. When I think that in this Dharma-ending age you alone, old layman, are a banner of light, and that this poor monk is old with no further days of receiving your teaching, what I look for is the future three assemblies of Longhua. This poor monk, bearing the sage’s grace, was granted a journey of ten thousand li; it was of no benefit to the Dharma-gate by a hair. Even the one move above I am unfit to raise before others. My good fortune is that in the eye of the teachings I have clarified the direct-pointing school: the three sūtras — the Laṅkāvatāra, the Śūraṅgama, and the Lotus — greatly overturn the ruts of words, and all have been printed; I entrust them to Ruding to seek your verification. Yet in Langya Mountain the wild fox lurks; I beg the diamond true eye to shine once and shatter the darkness — a great supporting condition for this Dharma.
To He Hanbo, Ministry of Revenue

In the mountains I received your letter and know that your taste for the Way deepens daily while worldly feeling recedes. You are giving your mind to the Laṅkāvatāra, swimming in the ocean of wisdom and observing the flow of delusive thoughts; in time the source will be clear and limpid. Thus you make of adverse conditions provisions for advancing on the Way. What is lacking is that you have no clear-eyed teacher of knowledge to keep you company and keep you awake, and I fear you are blocked by the words. In this great matter of sealing the mind by the teachings, be like a bee gathering from flowers: take only the nectar, do not harm the color. So whenever you read the scriptures or the encounter records of the ancient worthies, take in what your mind meets; what it does not meet, set aside. Do not force interpretations of your own; in time it will of itself become clear, and then word by word will silently accord with the true mind. Truly you need not make of not understanding an obstacle. Your nature is highly intelligent, and at this fine age your strength is more than enough; that you can gather yourself in so early means not only that you tread the broad highway but that it will be provision for blessing and long life. Heaven’s way of completing you is great. I hope you will take care of yourself, to answer my humble and deep hopes.
Reply to Wu Guanwo, Hanlin Academician

My karmic business in Wu and Yue was hurriedly concluded; because I could not bear the coming and going, I returned at once to Mount Kuang. Yet a settled dwelling in the mountains is far from easy to obtain: I entered the mountains seeking leisure, and instead became a burden to the mountain. In my declining years this suits me very ill. Let your nephew at Fudu shoulder it, and so spare you, old layman, anxiety. I am glad that the student-insects have been cleared away; did you indeed find a successor? The Dharma-gate is desolate: not only are clear-eyed masters hard to seek, but even among monks a man of true mind and real practice is rarely seen. How has the Dharma-gate come to such flatness? Your pure karma, old layman, is refined and pure, your taste of Dharma deepens daily, and the mind-light has begun to shine; you must already see through the ten directions. If there be occasion to meet and talk at leisure, that too would be a late fortune in this life.

These years in mountain dwelling, though far from the world, I often hear of alarms east and west, and cannot but be startled. Yet in the individual retribution there is surely fixed karma; still, the kalpa-calamities of living beings are bitter beyond hearing, and how much more for one who has himself passed through mud and fire? Since your mind, old layman, rests in the Pure Land, can you be without compassion? Heaven formed the great fortune of our dynasty: our Sage Founder’s virtue matched the Three and Five, his merit surpassed the hundred kings; the altars of state are long-enduring and should enjoy boundless years. But the karmic response of living beings cannot of itself be escaped. Often I think how the Dharma-gate has in one morning declined to this; looking back to its flourishing, it is hard to find again. I earnestly hold that the Huayan school is the fundamental Dharma-wheel of our Buddha, and that Qingliang is the ancestor of its composition in these lands; his commentary is precise and detailed, a grand model for ten thousand ages. Yet in its subcommentary, in the excess of seeking completeness, it is unavoidably too prolix, so that students gaze at the ocean and retreat. The scholar-officials prefer only the lucid brevity of the Combined Commentary, and by and large treat the other with enmity; and so doctrinal study too is about to fall silent. I have often said that the Combined Commentary is indeed direct, but it only clarifies the general purport; as for precise and detailed meaning in the text, it perhaps does not always hit the speaker’s intent. How I grieve that this great Dharma should be lost — what will become of the Dharma-eye in future? Not only will none roam the Dharma-realm and rest in contemplation of principle; even teachers of letters will be wholly lacking. From youth this rustic has kept his mind on this Dharma-gate; now, alas, he is old. Shutting the pass in the mountains, he has bent his attention to exhaustive study, wishing to look at the commentary alone, to draw out its essentials, discard the prolix and take the simple, and make the general purport clear, so as not to lose the author’s intent. Having set aside the subcommentary, I have also cut away its section divisions, and take directly what clarifies the root text, which seems easier to understand. Though it cannot be as grand and expansive as the Combined Commentary, yet in clarifying the sūtra through the commentary it happens to open up the speaker’s intent; where the commentary’s meaning is discontinuous, I occasionally venture my own humble view, seeking only that the veins run through, and not presuming to add anything of my own. This too is a place of repentance for this rustic in his old age, and a Dharma-offering made on behalf of those to come. Two years ago illness kept me from the effort; happily this year I am well, and the work is already seven or eight parts complete. I regret I cannot verify it face to face with you, old layman; I dare to send word of it, to give you one joy.

You have humbled me by showing me the story of Master Lang. This mountain monk has long admired the man, and regrets never having met him; I had long heard of his final move and held it great in my heart, though I did not know its beginning and end. Now, reading the stupa inscription and the records of his life and deeds, it surpasses what I had heard. You command me to write his biography — how could I add a single word? Yet the bond of the Dharma-gate I dare not decline. But to take Lanfeng as his mind-seal is, I fear, not what I have heard. This mountain monk once saw the man; he was called Iron Beak, and at the time all spoke of him as an outsider, one not received by the school. Even the single phrase about his encounter was not surpassing; it would be better to say that he had a place where the Dharma abode. Yet this too cannot exhaust Master Lang’s life. But when the affair of Zibai came, which was a great upheaval for the Dharma-gate, he remained calm and unmoved, and moreover praised Zibai as rare. In this one section lay Master Lang’s deep heart toward the Dharma-gate — he had the intent of Wang Zhu preserving Qi. To see him at the end seated on the jeweled throne and passing away shows him breathing through the same nostril as Zibai. Therefore in the biography I give weight to this alone. Master Lang in his stillness and light must surely count me a true friend. Yet a biography that is to be imperishable must have imperishable substance in it. Do you agree, old layman?
Reply to Wu Shengbai, Provincial Administration Commissioner

The monk from Caoxi arrived bearing your letter; I bowed, unrolled it, and read it three times, deeply indebted to your honored kindness. Your concern for the Dharma-way of the patriarch’s court, your pity for this foolish monk and your desire to rescue this famous mountain — how earnest and complete your heart is. Reading it, I could not but feel it pierce to my inmost being. When I think how this mountain monk has drifted on the sea of suffering for more than twenty years, and now happily rests his old age on Mount Kuang, where the surroundings are secluded and the mind still, so that all delusive thoughts have subsided and no other thought remains — and now you bid me, in deference to your honored kindness, take the Dharma-way of the patriarch’s court to heart, a duty of friendship I cannot decline. Yet the monastery on Mount Kuang was specially established for this mountain monk by the magistrates and benefactors as a place to retire, and its arrangements are not yet concluded; it is hard to leave lightly. If it were not properly settled, I would greatly fail the faith of the whole age, and that I cannot bear. Hence I hesitate and cannot decide clearly. I send this first to answer your command; when matters can be arranged suitably, I shall set out on the road.
Reply to Li Sanjin

You write that in cultivation one depends on teachers and friends — so it has always been. In essence, the practice lies with oneself; teachers and friends merely help to bring it out. As for the one needle, the one hammer-blow by which one suddenly penetrates: that is not the teacher’s or friend’s whole power, but one’s own work at one’s own portion being ripe, meeting the condition and being set off — the peck and the tap at the same instant. It is like a bell or drum: struck, it sounds. A block of wood or stone, though, would labor in vain. When Lingyun saw the peach blossom and awakened to the Way, when Xiangyan heard the bamboo struck and clarified his mind — what did they borrow from teacher or friend? For the most part the illness of students of the Way lies in a will that is not firm; next, in a solid self-view. With these two, one is like a sick man who spurns the doctor: even Lu and Bian can but fold their hands.
Reply to Shen Dajie

Zheng Baisheng came and told me that you have the will to shave your head. In my humble view I did not venture to think it certain; I did not expect that you could indeed be so brave and decisive. Yet you should ask your parents’ permission — this is the right principle in the Buddhadharma, and the hardest thing for them to grant gladly; this is the bodhisattva’s helping you to accomplish it. Of the six questions you sent, only the first two are urgent; the rest may wait. Weak with illness, I have forced myself to answer; I do not know whether they resolve your doubts. As to your wish to return home at once and keep the appointment at Fushui — though there is a place for protecting the Dharma there, I fear you would fall into the Chan of the nest and mortar. Your vow is vast; for the moment you need not emulate the ancients, but if you can take Yunqi as your model, forty years as one day, then the Dharma-ending age will look to you as yet another great banner of light.
Reply to Guo Qianqiu

You have entrusted me with your master’s stupa inscription; I am ashamed that, dull and muddled, I am not equal to your generous intent. Yet since the matter bears heavily on the Dharma-gate, I truly dare not fail to express my praise; nor may I earn blame by wild and baseless words, for a stupa inscription is the monastic history of its age, to be trusted a thousand years hence. In the ancient monastic histories and biographies there are Chan masters, whose line runs from the Sixth Patriarch down through the five houses; Dharma masters, whose line runs through Xianshou, Qingliang, and Tiantai in doctrine and contemplation; spirit-monks, whose line runs through Buddhayaśas and the various Indian masters and their extraordinary conduct; and eminent monks, whose line runs through the lofty conduct of Yuan, Zhi, Sheng, and Zhao. Beyond these four categories, others who established conditioned works of merit are not included. Your master’s pure cultivation and austerities have long been admired by this rustic. But when I read the life you brought, it does not seem to match what I have heard; I dare not let empty adornment burden his real virtue. So I take only his native colors: dwelling in the mountains, austerities, and pure integrity, with Buddha-recitation as his Dharma-gate throughout life. He should be ranked with Master Yuan, and placed among the eminent monks. Thus I dare to record briefly only his right conduct, taking trustworthiness as the main thing; by no means do I presume to slight or diminish him. Let your discernment decide. If it cannot be accepted, then do not carve it.
The Dream-Journey Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Nineteen
Preface to the Carving of the Fangce Edition of the Canon

In the autumn of the bingxu year of Wanli, the Great Master Daguan and Master Mizang Kai crossed the eastern sea at a distance and visited Qing at the Nāravaṇā cave, where they set out in full the karmic cause for re-carving the great canon in the fangce format, and made a covenant there in the cave. At that time Qing, deeply burdened with the Dharma, held his promises in earnest — how could he not shoulder it? But the cave door was not yet opened and the brambles not yet cleared, and he meant to wait for conditions. Afterward Master Da went west, and Masters Kai and Ben followed him to Qingliang to divine a dwelling and put questions to the Great One of Mañjuśrī’s chamber, and they received his seal of approval — the golden realm. Before long all conditions gathered. In the autumn of the gengyin year, Master Huanyu Ben came to me at Haiyin and showed Qing several fascicles of the Great Commentary of Zaobo that had been carved. Thereupon, burning incense and bowing, I bowed twice and received them. I rejoiced that the mind-ground Dharma was thoroughly penetrated, and the fragrance perfumed every pore. When I read the prefatory accounts by the great magistrates, elders, and laymen, which exhaust the beginning and end, and every word of which is true mind — truly nothing fails to flow from this Dharma-realm. They say too that the fangce format is akin to conventional truth, and that circulating it widely is a great skillful means; but they feared that those who cling to the palm-leaf format might raise doubts, and so explained at length and in full. What more is there to say? Alas, the confusion of human feeling is old: the number of those who lose their way is great. One may raise a jade ring again and again and still not awaken a single foolish bird, and how much less the great Way. Let me try to discuss it. When our Buddha, the Sage, taught the Dharma, he did so with the cloud-body of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, expounding the universal-gate Dharma-realm sūtra in accord with nature — dust speaks it, lands speak it, it blazes forth in speech. How could that be bounded by paper, ink, and letters, or circulated by seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving? What is transmitted today is only the lesser and greater transformation bodies’ forty-nine years and more than three hundred assemblies, the skillful means set out in accord with capacities, gathered in the dragon palace; even a master of the six penetrations could not exhaust their titles, but set out a small portion, dividing them into three baskets and twenty sections, spreading them widely in the Western Xia. What has flowed to these eastern lands is but a single leaf of the palm-leaf books. Entrusted for circulation, the various propagators of the Dharma established it according to place, bending to the needs of capacity. Hence it is said: in border lands one may speak the Four Noble Truths in the border tongue; or one may speak them in the common tongue; or manifest one’s own body, or another’s body; or show one’s own affairs, or another’s affairs — all such practices are the bodhisattva’s way. Consider how the good teachers who emerged from the Avataṃsaka all possessed birth-bodies, and each had his own Dharma-gate, none of them anything but what the oceanic-reflection samādhi and spiritual power of Vairocana manifest. Therefore conventional speech and the arts of livelihood all accord with the right Dharma. The Dharma is originally without abiding; meeting a condition, it becomes the teaching. So too the flowing water and the moving wind all proclaim the perfect sound, and the crying of birds and the chanting of apes all speak of non-duality. Green bamboo is suchness; yellow flowers are prajñā. How then could these be divided by the petty distinctions of Chinese and Sanskrit, or measured by the length of paper and felt? And yet — so the saying goes — human feeling settles into the customary and is confused by the rarely seen; why wonder at it? If at the start one had taken the Chinese-bound books as the covenant and the palm-leaf as not, and then made right and wrong of each other, that would truly be what is called “three in the morning.” Therefore the World-Honored One’s benefiting of beings lies wondrously in complying with capacity and occasion: in whatever body and by whatever Dharma one may be saved, in just that he saves and frees them. Thus, comply and they follow; oppose and they turn away — that is ordinary feeling. Now what this canon expounds is the Buddha’s true dharmakāya, the self-nature of all living beings. Alas for men, sunk and drunk in the dense forest of many sufferings, blind to it for so long. Therefore the World-Honored One swore: “I originally made a vow, wishing to cause all beings to be no different from me.” Without this, how could one see the Buddha-body, understand the self-nature, escape suffering and gain joy, and dwell where the Buddha dwells, to fulfill that vow? To save by this — if not by compliant skillful means, how could one cause true faith, and cause everyone to enter awakening by it? Moreover living beings have all kinds of desires and all kinds of inclinations; if the propagator of the Dharma complies with their desires and gives them what they like, none will fail to believe, rejoice, and be glad. Now the capacities to be transformed are the four assemblies. Reckoning the black-robed and the white-robed as distinct — like an ox that is black-horned and white-haired — and the Dharma that transforms as something to be monopolized: that is to cast in the black and reject the white, like taking the horns and discarding the hair. How is it one body seen as two? It shows our Dharma is not broad. Desiring thus to cause everyone to be saved, what hope is there? Moreover, in China it is said there is much thinking: where thinking is much, confusion is heavy; where confusion is heavy, wisdom is light; where wisdom is light, the faculties are dull. And so it is with all. How do we know it is so? Try observing the worldly-wise and eloquent: for the most part they are slaves of eye and ear, sunk in the mud of desire. Occasionally one with a numinous root planted in past lives, bearing the spirit of a hero, for the most part issues it in fame and rank, taking this and abandoning that. Even where prajñā weighs heavy within, still the Way does not overcome habit; so what is to be done — one hesitates in birth-and-death, which is truly painful. And in this Dharma-ending age those who receive the teaching are mostly puppets: how could they not have dull faculties? What the Dharma-gate depends on hangs by a single thread from a nine-cauldron weight. Outer trouble and inner anxiety are like Chu’s entry into Ying. Alas, alas. At such a time, who can rise with strength and rouse and save it? One like the Great Master: this act of carving is nothing less than the wail at the Qin court, and truly has the intent of seizing the enemy’s standard. His plan for restoring the Dharma-realm is far and great. Behold his outer protectors, like moats of gold — lofty, deep, firm, and sharp; are not such magistrates and laymen the host that welled up from the earth, who came having received the entrustment in person? Otherwise how could they be so brave and strong? So I look at ultimate truth: ultimate truth is not being. I look at conventional truth: conventional truth is not non-being. In this task we may set down our burden: it is like a cook who cannot manage the kitchen, while the invocator would step over the altar and vessels and do it for him. To exchange one for the other — would that not be unfortunate for both? And yet: do not say there is no one. Just consider what one has accumulated. I have heard that the great clod sighs and a myriad apertures rage and howl; because the sound is great, the echo is even. So one sings and ten thousand respond — like answering like; how could that be an empty saying? Know then that this task of the canon will count the days until the victory report; the merit of this carving will endure through vast kalpas without end. It will cause every person by it to see the Buddha, and every thing by it to clarify the mind; to behold the Dharma-realm at the tip of a hair, and meet Vairocana in the present moment. This may be called the supreme first principle of compliant skillful means, admired by gods and men, where the true and the conventional both return — a Dharma-gate of vast and awesome virtue. Someone may say: the fangce format reduces reverence — would that not be the offense of slighting the Dharma? I answer: the nature is serene, prajñā is perfect and bright; those who circulate it are like one lamp dividing into many. Even if the whole earth were set ablaze, no fuel is chosen yet the original fire is so of itself, neither increasing nor decreasing. Try taking this great torch of Dharma and making it pervade worlds as many as grains of sand, to the end of the future, burning up the icchantikas: even if the realm of living beings were emptied, this original Dharma would still be serene and ever-abiding. You two masters, press on, the banner before you. Alas, this petty one, ashamed in his Dharma-robe: the Chan bow is not drawn, the sword of wisdom is not keen, and being cowardly I dare not be first to mount. May I be permitted to follow with the whip.
Preface to the Great Canon in Fangce Format Requested by Master Qiao Zongshao of Jinghui Temple

Bodhidharma crossed the sea and came west, entering China by way of Wuyang; Patriarch Lu rose in Xinzhou, and the robe and bowl ended at Caoxi. Paramiti carried the Śūraṅgama Sūtra wrapped in his arm, and Minister Fang took it down in writing at Zhizhi. Thus the southern sea is the root ground of Chan and Buddhadharma. Why then, for a thousand years, has the transformation of the Way not spread, as though it were the time before the Buddha’s appearance, when no one knew what the Three Jewels were? When I first came here by the emperor’s grace, through adverse karma, and opened the Dharma at Qingmen, for a time black-robed and white-robed alike eagerly turned toward it, and the disciples of the Dharma-nature were mostly among the foremost. Within a few years the teaching spread greatly; truly, if one would understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, one should observe the time and the karmic conditions. At that time Master Qiao Zongshao, a disciple of Jinghui, resolved to form a society in emulation of the old Donglin precedent, devoting himself to the pure karma; for more than ten years it has been as one day. Lately, because the teaching was not yet widespread and what he had seen and heard was not broad, he wished to request the great canon, to benefit gods and men universally. It happened that I had just returned to Caoxi; the master bowed, took up incense, and set the whole matter out. I heard it and said with joy: the Buddha-nature in men’s minds is like the water in the great earth, like the echo in a hollow valley; it need not be sought elsewhere but is originally possessed. And yet, though the water is originally there, one must dig to be moistened by it; though the echo has no form, one must call before it answers. It is like the pearl in the poor man’s clothing: blind to it, he does not know; he must rely on kin and friends to point it out, and then he opens his collar and gains the benefit. Thus the master’s forming a society and reciting the Buddha’s name is like the man who digs the well; and his requesting the great canon now is like the kin and friends who point out the pearl. If each gains the benefit of the crossing, the point lies in the moment when a man opens his collar and loosens his belt; it is not the master who gives it, but truly the master who points it out. Thus it will pass on and on without end, and one will see the transformation of Kapilavastu spread across the edge of the southern seas. Reckoning its merit, how could it be conceived or discussed?
Preface to the Comprehensive Discussion of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra is the great dhāraṇī gate and secret mind-seal of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. It governs the whole canon of one treasury: the five periods and three vehicles, sage and commoner, true and false, delusion and awakening, cause and effect, gathering all dharmas without omission. The gradations of cultivation and realization, right and wrong; the circumstances of turning about in cyclic existence — all are clear before the eyes like a fruit in the palm. It may be called the fathoming of the source of the one mind and the encompassing of the purport of all dharmas; no sūtra is more vast and complete than this. The Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of one great matter; apart from this there is no other guidance. Those who classify the teachings and confine it to one period or one teaching — are they not peering through a tube and measuring the sea with a shell? Since it entered these lands, its interpreters number more than ten houses. Beyond the Combined Explanation, in recent times black-robed and white-robed have each produced their own eyes and hands, and more than one has propagated it widely. In opening the text and explaining the meaning, all have been precise and thorough, revealing all without remainder; what need was there for feet to the snake? But in reviewing all their sayings, there are points that do not satisfy me: only the contemplation of principle has not been brought into accord. Thus though the sentences are clear, the great purport is not yet fluent, and students cannot escape the sigh of the blind men and the elephant. In the past I dwelt among the ice and snow of Mount Wutai, investigating the one road above, and used this sūtra to verify and seal my mind; fixing the right mind firmly to illumine it, I came to an open clarity and attainment.
