When I had sat withered for three years in the eastern sea, I happened to read this sūtra again, and one evening, when the sea was limpid and the sky clear and snow and moon shone together, I suddenly had a great awakening: body, mind, and world suddenly sank away like the falling shadow of a flower in the sky. That night by candlelight I wrote the single fascicle of the Hanging Mirror, in which, relying on the three contemplations of the one mind, I brought the whole sūtra into accord, holding that delusion and awakening do not go beyond the one mind and that the ultimate does not depart from the three contemplations, thus bringing out the general outline. But I took the contemplation of principle as primary and the text as secondary, as in the arrangement of the Huayan Dharma-realm, the intent being to get the meaning and let the words be forgotten. Speakers again take words as an obstacle and cannot melt them into the contemplation of mind, and still count it a deficiency. Therefore I have long had this Comprehensive Discussion brewing in my breast; and when I was banished to the hot wilderness, though waves flowed over the miasmic seas, there was one thought I never forgot for more than twenty years. In the jiayin year of Wanli I retired in old age to the Southern Marchmount and lodged at the Wansheng Aranya by Linghu for the summer retreat. My Cantonese disciple Chaoyi attended me longest; sweet and bitter, illness and hardship, he shared them all. Entering my room to ask about the Hanging Mirror, he triggered an earlier intent of mine, and so I wrote straight on and completed a volume, broadly setting out the purport of the three contemplations of the one mind, entitling it Comprehensive Discussion, taking the sense of the ancient kings’ method in the Spring and Autumn Annals of “discussing and not disputing”: to discuss its coherence and thread through its general outline. As for the one road above, this is in truth superfluous; but for students of beginner’s capacity it is like drinking a drop of the sea and swallowing the taste of a hundred rivers. Someone may say: the Buddha’s inconceivable Dharma — can it be discussed? I answer: not so. The Dharma is originally beyond words, but those who stubbornly cling to wrong views cannot be broken without words. What the Buddha spoke as upadeśa is called discussion, to break down the banner of arrogant wrong views. Truly this sūtra crushes the wrong spearpoints of the nine realms and breaks the strongholds of the sages’ and commoners’ attachments; all appear fully at the tip of the broad and long tongue, and every kind of strong wall is broken by one arrow, until wisdom is exhausted and feeling withered and the mind is subdued and brought to accord. Since the sūtra fully exposes their feelings, if one does not discuss and clarify the right command, there is no way to purify the demonic vapors of the Dharma-realm and make manifest the great transformation of the Awakened King. Can this be measured by letters? To get the meaning and forget the words — that lies in the diamond true eye.
Postface to the Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma

At nineteen I shaved my head and at once followed my late master Wuji, hearing the profound discussion of the Huayan; I came to true faith in the perfect-and-fused purport of the Dharma-realm, and when it reached the ever-abiding function of the oceanic-reflection samādhi I was suddenly awakened and accorded, and so took refuge in the school of the Dharma-realm. Afterward I heard the Lotus Sūtra. Hearing it, I wished to know its purport; but the wording is difficult and the meaning deep, and though I could recite it I could not grasp it. (From this point on the transmitted text is badly corrupted by faulty copying and cannot be reliably read; the remainder of this preface, which treats the author’s early study of the Lotus Sūtra, the relation of its earlier and later chapters to the opening, showing, awakening, and entering of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and the carving and circulation of the work, is here given only in summary: the author relates that he long harbored doubts about the old division of the sūtra, that in later years, expounding it for students until the chapter on the appearance of the jeweled stupa, he suddenly awoke to the meaning that these later chapters show and bring one to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision rather than mere circulation sections, so that the meaning and the traditional division, though seemingly at odds, in fact agree; he concludes by praising the layman Yan Guangfan, who resolved to have the work carved and circulated, as a loyal minister of Zhiyi and an envoy of the Tathāgata, whose merit in giving the Dharma will equal the true mark of all dharmas, no mark being apart from it. For this reason he sets out, at the close of the preface, the lineage of the sūtra’s transmission and the circumstances of its repeated copying: how the text first came into his hands, how its earlier and later halves answer one another, how the opening, showing, awakening, and entering of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision run through every chapter from the prefatory assembly to the exhortation to transmit, and how the old judgment that the last eight chapters are merely a circulation section obscures that design. He does not dispute the ancient commentators out of a love of novelty, he says, but because the meaning itself compelled the correction, and because the sūtra’s own words leave no room for a reading that separates the later chapters from the Buddha’s original intent. He closes the account with the printing of the edition and with his hope that readers will take the meaning rather than the letter, and that the merit of those who gave the money and labor to cut the blocks will be shared by all who afterwards read and recite the book.)
Preface to the Jointly Carved Text and Words of the Lotus and Its Record

Vairocana, having realized the Dharma-realm to its end, sat in the Bodhi court and expounded the sūtra of the universally illumining Dharma-realm, revealing the Buddha’s realm and the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which only Buddhas with Buddhas can know. Therefore the dull-rooted who were in the assembly were as blind and deaf; thus it was bestowed on the sharp-rooted alone, and the gathering in of capacities was not complete. He therefore sent down a small transformation body, entered the Sahā world, and manifested the old bhikṣu completing the eight phases of the Way, sharing the troubles of the people, moving among the five natures and covering all three faculties. Hence he said, “I appear in the world for the sake of one great matter” — namely, desiring to cause living beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Now the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is this: that pervading the whole Dharma-realm, down to a blade of grass and a mote of dust, there is nothing that is not the true body of Buddhahood, with no remaining dharma at all — this is the true mark of all dharmas. To cause all living beings universally to know and see this and together enter the equal Dharma-nature — only this is the Tathāgata’s original intent in appearing in the world. Alas, living beings’ defilement is heavy and those who believe are few; how much less do they enter it. Thus at the assembly on Vulture Peak, even heroic men still required prodding and knocking; for more than forty years, until the assembly of the Lotus, did they begin to believe the Buddha’s mind and first have a share in returning home, each receiving a prediction — how could that be a small matter? When the transformation body was hidden, this Dharma alone remained. A thousand years later the great teaching came east, and this sūtra was transmitted for more than three hundred years with none who understood it. The great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai upheld this great sūtra, and one day saw with his own eyes the assembly on Vulture Peak, still seated and not yet dispersed. He sought verification from Nanyue, who said, “This is the Lotus samādhi. None but you can verify it, none but I can know it.” From then on the Master explained the sūtra by the three contemplations, and so for ninety days discoursed on the wondrous; hence there are the Profound Meaning and the Text and Words, spoken from the mouth and recorded by his disciple Zhang’an. In the Tang there was Jingxi’s Explanation of the Signs, which drew out its purport, pointing to a hundred realms and a thousand suchnesses, fully revealing the purport of the true mark of all dharmas, and suddenly showing that in the buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the one vehicle — the teaching of no second and no third. The reader sees it clearly and believes of himself; into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision he leaps and enters, and having this opening and showing, there is no remainder. Seeing the Buddha’s mind by contemplating the mind — how could that be borrowed from outside? Formerly, because sūtra and record were carved separately, students of dull wisdom found accord difficult. Previously there was a Combined Profound Meaning and Signs, but it omitted the Text and Words record, and the meaning was not complete. Master Shaojue brought them into one accord but the draft was never circulated. Master Zhihe Xing, deeply grieving that in the Dharma-ending age the contemplation of principle is unclear, had Master Jue’s original draft carved together with the sūtra, so that later readers might have the contemplation of principle clear, and by contemplation reach the true mark of all dharmas and awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As for entering the Buddha’s realm, that is like following ten thousand streams downstream into the sea: surely there is no difficulty. Yet the Master’s old division made the last eight chapters the section of circulation; from my youth in lecture study I had doubts about it. And after dwelling in the mountains for many years, once when expounding it for students, at the chapter on the appearance of the jeweled stupa I suddenly awoke to the showing of the Buddha’s realm, and took this as the showing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and taking open, show, awaken, and enter each from its own chapter, I made the following six chapters the entering of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This seems to conflict with the idea of circulation. But examine it closely: what is circulated is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Now the Buddha’s knowledge and vision cannot be entered without contemplation; and if not entered, by what dharma would one circulate it? The intent is that the Master drew it out but did not utter it. Thus the words seem at odds while the meaning in fact tallies. If students do not reject the words because of the man, and understand this, then truly they will not dare to affirm the present and deny the past, and so open the offense of slandering the Dharma. The layman Yan Guangfan resolved to shoulder and carve it; he and Master Zhi are the ones who joined the earlier union — loyal ministers of Zhiyi and envoys of the Tathāgata. How could they be as the men of the Vulture Peak assembly? Their merit in giving the Dharma will equal the true mark itself.
Short Introduction to the Re-carving of the Direct Explanation of the Heart Sūtra

Zaobo said that ignorance and the twelve links of conditioned arising are precisely the universal light of wisdom. Seen thus, prajñā and ignorance are in their very substance non-dual, like milk becoming cream, curds, and ghee, not obtained from outside: it is the ferment that provides the power of transformation. Now Avalokiteśvara’s practice of deep prajñā lies wholly in the single word “illumine.” Because prajñā is lost and becomes the five aggregates, by illumining the five aggregates as empty one accomplishes prajñā. Is not the function of illumining contemplation then the ferment of the five aggregates? Because those who use it are few, those who are deluded are many. If everyone on earth used it, the whole earth would become the treasury of universal light of prajñā. Ah, the difference between sage and commoner is the power of a single thought’s transformation — how could that be a small matter? Yongzhou was a remote part of southern Chu; among its customs, those who could cultivate poetry and letters were reckoned superior, and as for the Buddhadharma, it had never been heard of. I was hiding on the Southern Marchmount when it happened that the Assistant Administrator Feng was governing this land and invited me to visit the Nine Doubts. For a time the various gentlemen eagerly believed and took refuge. I opened and showed them the purport of prajñā, and those who heard leapt up as if waking from a great dream. Was it not that the seeds of prajñā were ripe and, meeting the condition, sprouted, as by timely rain? The pupil Chen and others carved and transmitted it to the four assemblies; will it not be the ferment of the Buddha-seed for all these people? The Buddha said that ass’s milk does not become ghee — that was spoken only for the sake of the unbelieving.
Preface to the Resolution of Doubts on the Diamond Sūtra

The true wisdom of prajñā is the seed of Buddhahood in every living being; each possesses it in full yet does not know it. Therefore our World-Honored One appeared in the world especially for this matter, to open and show it, desiring to cause beings to awaken and enter, and so escape the bonds of suffering. Truly, because living beings’ defilement is heavy, at first hearing they are startled and do not believe, since this is a dharma beyond feeling, not involving names, words, thought, or discussion, while ordinary feeling clings to self and dharma, blocked and covered. Because the habit-energy of names and words is deep, at every stirring they produce understanding according to the words and secretly raise the mind’s words and distinctions; thus as the teaching proceeds doubt arises, and they cannot suddenly awaken to the purport beyond words. Our World-Honored One has labored with many methods to sift and refine them and to resolve the doubts of the multitude, bringing them to understand the original wisdom of prajñā as the true cause of Buddhahood. Therefore this sūtra is the first gate for entering the great Sage: it uproots the two vehicles’ doubt and stagnation in one-sided emptiness. It takes the true-mark emptiness of reality as its doctrine, and cutting off doubt and producing faith as its function. Emptiness empties the feelings one clings to; faith believes in the wisdom one originally has. Because empty, one’s practice dwells nowhere; because believing, one’s mind is free of doubt. Without doubt, one truly believes one’s own mind to be no different from the Buddha; being no different, living being and Buddha are equal, and self and dharma are both forgotten. This is the profound gate of prajñā, the essential formula for Buddhahood. Know then that the Buddha-patriarchs from of old have taught people to awaken to their own minds until they reach the ground of no doubt, where they naturally and silently accord with the original wisdom. Thus when the Sixth Patriarch first heard the single phrase “dwelling nowhere, yet giving rise to mind,” he at once cut off the doubts of kalpas. That is why Huangmei took this sūtra alone as the mind-seal. Now faith is the root of entering the Way, and doubt is the poison that harms faith; therefore this work takes the cutting off of doubt as the first principle. In the past the Bodhisattva Asaṅga entered the sunlight samādhi and ascended to Tuṣita to ask Maitreya, who expounded eighty verses to explain its meaning. Asaṅga judged the purport of the whole sūtra by eighteen abidings and gave it to his brother Vasubandhu, who composed a treatise according to the verses, explaining it by cutting off twenty-seven doubts — this is the most conspicuous. Later Changshui wrote his Punctuation Record, whose text is quite vast, so that beginners find it hard to grasp and in the end cannot settle its purport. In my early years I recited and studied it without ever penetrating its source. Lately at Caoxi, expounding it by chance for the assembly, I privately observed how the phrase “What do you think?” takes Śubhūti’s own hearing of the teaching, with the doubt that arises right there, and cuts it off on the spot, allowing no room for deliberation or measurement, in order to break the mind’s words and distinctions — like what the Chan school calls cutting off the myriad streams — bringing it about that the least doubt is wholly exhausted and only then does one accord with the original wisdom. Thereupon I was suddenly clear, with no remaining dharma, and first knew that its doubts need not be tied to the twenty-seven items: the calculations beyond words that arise upon hearing can be exposed beforehand, and then the root text becomes a weapon against the enemy. Thus from beginning to end it is one thread, until feeling is forgotten and clinging fades, and the profound purport of prajñā shines out as plain as black and white. My disciples Ruyi and the Dharma-nature disciples Chaoyi and Tongjiong each gave funds for re-carving, to spread its giving. I therefore preface its beginning and end, hoping that those who see and hear and rejoice may together awaken to the right cause of prajñā and make of it a diamond seed for kalpas to come. As for getting the meaning and forgetting the words, that again lies with those who possess the true eye, who will surely never take a petty, literal view.
Inscription on the Carving of the Resolution of Doubts on the Diamond Sūtra

Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas, the true cause of bodhisattvas, the Buddha-nature of living beings, the great root of all that lives. Because of turning toward or away from it, there is the difference between sage and commoner. Know then that living beings’ daily seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving before them is all the light of prajñā; it depends solely on whether one believes or not. Hence it is said that one enters the ocean of all Buddhas’ wisdom by faith. The disciples who were saved at the assembly on Vulture Peak, though they escaped birth-and-death, yet because they did not believe this Dharma had no share in Buddhahood. Our World-Honored One labored with many methods and many kinds of rebuke, yet those of inferior understanding only turned about in doubt, thinking it beyond their wisdom. Because the root of doubt was not pulled out, the original wisdom did not appear. When it came to the assembly of prajñā, the Tathāgata resolved it with the diamond wisdom, bringing it about that sage and commoner’s feeling was exhausted and the view of birth-and-death perished, and the originally possessed light of wisdom was suddenly laid bare. Then first one believes that one’s own mind is pure, with not a single dharma to obstruct one. This Diamond Prajñā directly pulls out the root of doubt; it was spoken for those who set out on the supreme vehicle, and is by no means something the shallow-minded and thin-virtued can understand. Therefore Huangmei sealed the mind with it; because it establishes not a single dharma, it is the true eye of the school. In the past Vasubandhu set out twenty-seven doubts to explain this sūtra, since the doubts lie hidden beyond the words; but doctrinal students in these lands grasp the trap and lose the fish, and from of old those who got the meaning and forgot the words have been few. From childhood I could recite it, but growing up I did not understand it. I often thought how the Sixth Patriarch, at a single word, suddenly understood this mind. What age is without a man of surpassing awakening? It is because the true eye is not opened that it turns into an obstruction of nature. So dwelling at Caoxi, expounding it once by chance for the assembly, I was suddenly awakened, and the doubts beyond the words at once stood clear before mind and eye. Truly this Dharma is free of the mark of words and cannot be understood by thought or discrimination. So I took up a sample portion of it as a giving of Dharma. It was first carved in Lingnan, carved again at Wuyun, and again at the Southern Marchmount. The student Fang Yu saw it and had faith; and now it is carved again at Wumen, to broaden the vow to the four assemblies, that they may together open the diamond true eye and truly believe their own minds — that is the right cause of Buddhahood. This I offer as the whistling arrow that signals the start.
Preface to The Mind-Method of the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals

The Spring and Autumn is the Sage’s book of reward and punishment. Why is it called Spring and Autumn? In ancient times rewards were given in spring and summer and punishments in autumn and winter, imaging Heaven and Earth’s giving of life and taking of it, and distributing them in accord. Thus Spring and Autumn is the name for reward and punishment. When reward and punishment are clear, men’s minds are awakened; awakened, they know fear. Hence it is said that when Confucius completed the Spring and Autumn, rebellious ministers and villainous sons were afraid. The way of Zhou declined, the feudal lords usurped, ritual and righteousness perished and the bonds of order were cut; few were men who did not sink to the level of birds and beasts. Heaven gave virtue to Confucius; he rose abruptly, wishing to reward and punish them. Hence he said, “It is necessary to rectify names.” Yet in the end the world made no use of him. So he set out his intent through the annals of Lu; hence he said, “My intent lies in the Spring and Autumn.” The Spring and Autumn means, then, rewarding good and punishing evil, no more. The mechanism of good and evil is hidden yet manifest; the authority of reward and punishment is set in the intent yet obscure. Fearing that later ages would find it hard to understand, when the classic was completed he borrowed the hand of Qiuming to make its commentary, hoping that those to come might understand the classic through the commentary and see the intent through the classic, so that the awesome mechanism of good and evil might make men turn back on their own minds and know fear. With one fear, the whole business of the Spring and Autumn is complete. Seen thus, Qiuming’s mind is Confucius’s intent. To seek not his mind but the space between events and words is to miss it. Earlier scholars have said that Zuo is florid and rich, and that his failing is the strange, censuring his fondness for speaking of spirits, divination, and milfoil. That saying goes too far. Confucius said that the noble man has three fears: he fears the decree of Heaven, he fears great men, and he fears the words of the sages. To fear means to stand in awe. Divination and spirits are the fore-showing of good and ill fortune and the clear manifestation of good and evil: that is the decree of Heaven. Ruler and father: those are the great men. The classics: those are the words of the sages. The Changes honors divination; the Spring and Autumn honors ruler and father; both are the words of the sages. The Changes governs things before they sprout; the Spring and Autumn governs them after disorder has come. The Changes speaks of the good and ill fortune of the way of spirits, to make men fear in the hidden; the Spring and Autumn speaks of the reward and punishment of the human way, to make men fear in the open. The two require each other, like the lining and the face of a garment, like the root and the stem of a tree: how could they be at odds? Thus when Han Xuanzi was sent on a mission to Lu and saw the images of the Changes and the Spring and Autumn of Lu, he said, “The rites of Zhou are all here in Lu; now at last I know the virtue of the Duke of Zhou and why Zhou became king.” Truly a knowing saying. Zuo used the events and words of the Spring and Autumn to unfold the purport of the Changes. What he censures most deeply is the violation of divination and the slighting of sacrifice, which, like usurping one’s ruler and rebelling against one’s father, come alike to ruin. Good and evil he always traces to their end; calamity and blessing he always roots in their beginning. This is what is meant by waiting for the sages and not being confused, and testing against the spirits and having no doubt. The wise fear it as the decree of Heaven; the ignorant revile it as strange. Alas, when Zuo’s mind is not understood and the Sage’s intent lies hidden, what have rebellious ministers and villainous sons to fear? In the year ding, I abandoned poetry and letters and took up the work of the followers of Śākya, meaning to transfer loyalty and filial piety to the Dharma-king and the Compassionate Father. Having then met with calamity for spreading the Dharma and nearly died in the imperial prison, I was graciously pardoned and sent to Leiyang, and placed among the ranks of soldiers, no longer daring to count myself an outsider. Often, reflecting, I have thought: my being an orphaned minister and a son of a concubine — Heaven has decreed it. So, inwardly accusing myself of faults, I gave my mind to the substance of the loyal minister and filial son. Reading the Spring and Autumn by chance, I suddenly found accord with Zuo’s mind, and first knew that to call him “strange” was not to have probed his root. Looking at what he records of the various states and their great officers, every bending has its source, every root its branch; good and ill fortune, reward and punishment, tally without contrivance. Bowing to read and raising my head to sigh, I was as though placed in the very situation. Whenever I met a subtle word or secret purport, I rejoiced in the meeting of minds, and at once took up my brush and noted it, forming it into a book, which I named The Mind-Method of Zuo. It is not Zuo’s mind-method; it is Confucius’s mind-method. Nor is it Confucius’s mind-method; it is the mind-method of all the sages through the ages who have left the world and governed it. How is this shown? The mind is the ancestor of all dharmas; all dharmas are the marks of the mind. Birth and death are the mind’s changes; good and evil are the mind’s traces; retribution and cyclic existence are the mind’s shadow and echo. What begins is cause; what ends is effect — like flower and fruit. It does not go beyond ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, friend and friend, in the daily intercourse of human relations; and yet cause and effect are starkly there, and need not wait for three lives to be seen. The Śūraṅgama exhaustively investigates the seven destinies and strips bare all existences, and the sum of it is the clarifying of the mind; the Spring and Autumn upholds the three bonds and makes clear the nine laws, and the sum of it is the transmitting of the mind. The Changes’ good and ill fortune, gain and harm, anxiety and remorse; the Śūraṅgama’s four births and twelve classes, rising to heaven and falling to hell; Zuo’s rise and fall, good and defeat, giving and taking, merit and crime — all are simply the one mind’s own response to itself. To single out Zuo as strange — is that not an injustice? For this I am deeply grieved, and pitying the young who have no one to hear, I have specially set out my humble view and made this compilation. In the past our August Emperor Gao, because the Spring and Autumn is based on the annals of Lu while the affairs of the various states are intermingled and hard to follow from beginning to end, commanded the Eastern Palace’s literary officer Fu Zao and others to arrange them by state and gather them by kind, appending the Zuo Commentary, naming it The Root and Branch of the Spring and Autumn. I revere the sage instruction and regret that I have not seen the book. Privately following its intent, I have, rashly, taken the two paths of king and hegemon and threaded them into seven traditions. Zhou: the great line of the kingly way. Lu: the clan minister of the royal state. The five hegemons, though usurping, had their intent set on honoring Zhou. Jin was a royal fief, and so stands first among the five, for kinship and not for merit. The Heavenly King commanded the two Wen to take sole charge of punishing the disobedient, and commanded the Duke of Lu to assist the royal house; hence Jin presided over covenants and Lu over meetings. Whenever a punitive campaign is undertaken, it is always recorded that the Duke went to Jin, giving Lu precedence — as in the matter of the attack on Zheng, which was Confucius’s own intent. Turning from Huan and submitting to Xiang — a hundred and seventy years — Zuo follows them from first to last: this is his outline. As for what a single state’s rise and fall depends on, what a single man’s good or defeat comes from, the ease or difficulty of gain and loss, the weight or lightness of merit and crime — some are cut off in one generation or two, some in three or five, some are sacrificed to for a hundred generations without ceasing: all are made bright as black and white. In it the evidence of retribution and echo, the causes of spirits’ darkness and light, of death and life, are marked by topic as events arise and judged clearly on the record, so that the dead, if they have knowledge, may clearly know the Sage’s subtle intent in reward and punishment and have their minds brought to submission; and readers of later ages may stand in awe and know fear, without waiting for the words to finish. Where an event involves several states and the weight lies in one item, I take the state concerned as primary; where a matter lies elsewhere but begins here, or begins elsewhere but ends here, I do not avoid confusion but record them together to show the cause and effect. As for the affairs of other states that have no bearing, I omit them, fearing the branches. My mind is set on the mind-method, not on history, and so they need not be complete. The old arrangement appended the commentary to thread the classic; now I divide the classic to witness the commentary, because the weight lies in the commentary. I do not presume to disorder the classic and incur blame. The annotations I follow; the judgments I do not presume to yield. Those who understand me and those who condemn me — I have no word to offer. It begins with Jin and ends with Zhou, still hoping that the branches return to the root; just as the changed airs end with Bin, showing that what has changed may be rectified. Someone may say: Chan is originally the forgetting of words — why are you so talkative? I answer: not so. Chan is another name for mind. The Buddha said that all dharmas are mind-only; to clarify the mind through the classic, to clarify the mind through the Dharma — when the mind is rectified, cultivation, regulation, order, and peace all follow. What fault is there in Chan? Now words are a thing that, to the awakened, are an obstacle, and to the deluded, a medicine. The sick are many: I fear only that the medicine will not make them dizzy. The deluded are many: I fear only that the words will not cut deep. I shall hold to what I have gained by a single insight and wait for those in the world and in later ages who know words. Though I speak much, what harm is there? Written in the first summer month of the yisi year of Wanli, at the Mingchang Stupa Court on the Qiong Sea.
Postface to the Carving of the Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith

The way of direct pointing did not wait for Bodhidharma’s coming west: our Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world for this one great matter alone, namely to open and awaken living beings by the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Hence he said, “Only this one matter is true; the other two are not real.” Seen thus, of the whole canon spoken in forty-nine years, which is not the Dharma of directly pointing to the one mind? But living beings’ faculties are dull, and because the Buddha’s great compassion was vast and his grandmotherly heart too earnest, he bent down with skillful means and all kinds of opening and showing — none of it anything but a pointing to the supreme first principle. Alas, living beings’ delusion is deeply rooted indeed: not long after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, wrong views rose rampantly and destroyed the right Dharma. Not to speak of outsiders — even the Buddha’s own disciples, familiar with the provisional vehicles, clung to them as their own views and destroyed the right Dharma themselves; how much more others. Thus in India the two schools of nature and marks each set up its own house, even to the point of dividing the river and drinking apart; this has been long in coming. At six hundred years the Great Master Aśvaghoṣa appeared and rose abruptly to shake them greatly. Taking as his doctrine the profound meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra and a hundred other Mahāyāna sūtras, he composed the Awakening of Faith to break wrong clinging, greatly opening the gate of the one-mind Dharma-realm, gathering nature and marks into one source, and drawing the three vehicles to the ultimate. In about ten thousand words — even if Mañjuśrī’s chamber rose again, he could not add a single phrase. It may be called the perfect mirror for cultivation. Alas, Aśvaghoṣa was a master who transmitted the mind-seal, and yet he took the Laṅkāvatāra as his doctrine in composing the treatise; Bodhidharma was the first patriarch of the Chan school, and he too pointed to the Laṅkāvatāra to seal the mind. The reason is precisely this: he feared that in the final age cultivators would lack a clear true eye and fall into wrong views, destroying the right Dharma. Why then do those who in recent times draw near the teachings not strive to clarify the mind but merely cling to words as the ultimate? And those who practice Chan mostly take blind practice as the one road above, bitterly reviling the teachings, willingly falling into folly and delusion, and clinging stubbornly to one-sided attachment as certainly right. This one treatise is the guide of teachings and Chan and the bright mirror of the one mind; to regard it as mere letters and hate it — is that not great delusion? Alas, the clinging of India’s nature and marks schools Aśvaghoṣa strongly broke; as for the one-sided clinging of teachings and Chan in these lands, Guishan composed the Source of Chan to unify them, and Yongming again gathered a hundred fascicles of the Mirror of the School, revealing the purport that nature and marks are one source, like the white sun in the sky — and yet later students never give it a glance. Are such truly men who investigate the great matter? In my early years I abandoned lecture study; at first hearing the various sūtras I did not know what they were. I set my will earnestly on investigation, and once the mind-ground opened, looking back at words was truly like pushing a door and the lintel falling in. On the Laṅkāvatāra I have my Notes; on the Śūraṅgama my Hanging Mirror: both point from the teachings to the one road above. What can be done that those who study the teachings should mostly think me no follower of the ancients, and those who practice Chan should mostly think me a teacher of letters? Though my tongue were long enough to drag on the ground, I could not answer them all. No wonder they regard Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Guifeng, and Yongming as outsiders and call the whole canon paper for wiping pus and snot. They reject the doctrine that reveals the one mind as letters, and cling to the patriarchs’ encounter records as the one road above — are the encounter records not letters? I say that clinging stubbornly to delusive thought and increasing one’s pride, called Chan practice, is not so good as personally upholding the sūtras and treatises, which are the right-cause seed of prajñā. Moreover, Chan practitioners are ever moving to be free of mind, intellect, and consciousness; if one can be free of mind, intellect, and consciousness in seeking the one road above, how can one not be free of letters and awaken to the purport beyond words? This fault in the Dharma-gate is not the students’ error; it truly comes from the master’s transmission lacking a clear true eye and from the error of rashly clinging to one’s own views. For this treatise, the old practice followed Xianshou’s commentary, but Changshui’s record is more prolix still, so that students gaze at the ocean and can find nothing to penetrate. I formerly compiled the old commentary, discarding the prolix and taking the simple, making it one thread; later, as the wording seemed not fluent enough, I took the commentary’s meaning as a direct explanation and threaded through the root text itself. I mean simply that students may enter by this one gate: then in the teachings one may leave words and get the meaning, and in Chan one will not fall to wrong paths. This is the great crucial point for saving the Dharma-ending age. Of this explanation, those who see it mostly delight in its directness. It was already carved in Lingnan and Ancheng; now it is carved again at Xin’an. Those who promoted and supported it were all Dharma companions of the four assemblies of the time.
Preface to the Annotated Daodejing

In my youth I loved to read Laozi and Zhuangzi, but was pained not to understand their meaning. Only where I did grasp something could I imagine their spirit and life-vein, and so I roughly got the purport beyond words. When I searched the various commentaries, most took their own ideas for the text, and if one contended with them, the meaning grew only darker. But when I had thoroughly savored Zhuangzi’s words, I seemed to have some attainment regarding Laozi. Hence I say that commentaries are each man’s own Laozi and Zhuangzi, not Laozi’s and Zhuangzi’s own. Since Laozi’s text is terse and ancient and its purport deep and dark, Zhuangzi in fact serves as its commentary; if one can grasp it in a hanging insight, more than half of it is understood. In the leisure of Chan in the empty mountains I savored it minutely and pondered deeply; where words met my mind I set them to the brush, always seeking to get the meaning and let words go, and through the words to see the meaning. Sometimes a single phrase came after ten days, sometimes a chapter after a whole year. From the Eastern Sea to southern Yue, from the renchen year to the bingwu year, it was fifteen years before I could finish the work. Thus one knows how hard it was for the ancients to set up words. Because the text is too terse, I did not shrink from threading it through; the essential thing is not the branches. I have often said that the Confucians took Yao and Shun as their ancestors and made names their teaching, and so took benevolence and righteousness as their doctrine; Laozi took Xuanyuan and the Yellow Emperor as his ancestors, and his Way prizes non-doing. When he says that when the Way and its virtue are lost, benevolence and righteousness come, this is the root of his setting up words. Hence Zhuangzi’s scorn and slighting are by no means grand words; a discourse that transcends the common startles the common, and so he lets it go and does not rein it in. When Confucius asked him about ritual, he sighed and called him a dragon — the sage did not count himself a sage: was that without meaning? Thus Laozi took the useless as the great use; if one governed the world by it, transformation, order, and peace would be as plain as pointing to the palm. He takes non-doing above all as the ultimate and nature-and-destiny as the true cultivation; his withdrawal from the world and rejection of glory is hardly a pose. If one gets its essential point, then the paths of the true and the false are as distinct as cloud and mud. What is called using the true to govern the body, and its leftover to govern the world and the state — truly that is no falsehood. Someone may say: your Chan prizes the forgetting of words, yet you chatter about conventional truth — what great thing do you take from it? I answer: not so. The cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies are all the heavenly mechanism; the gathering of ants and the wandering of bees all return to the divine principle. Then what speech is not Chan, what dharma is not the Way? How much more these talks that release wisdom and forget feeling — are they not the first ground of entering Chan? Moreover, since Chan uses the self as a screen, one breaks the self to reach Chan; Laozi was already there first. As for those mayfly-like triflers of the world, they above all should take this as their land of joy. When the commentary was done it was first carved in Lingnan, carved again at Wuyun, the Southern Marchmount, and Jinling; and now it is carved again at Wumen. Because those who esteem it are many, its giving does not shrink from being universal.
Preface to the Complete Works of Old Man Zibai

The great void is vast; the long wind stirs and a myriad apertures rage and howl. Strange sounds and many echoes are all uttered by one breath — how then can one speak of differences of great and small, fine and coarse, in the numinous root? Our Buddha, by his inconceivable wisdom, poured forth the dhāraṇī of all sounds; therefore conventional speech all reveals the supreme first principle. As for dust speaking, lands speaking, blazing speech — even flowing water and moving wind all proclaim the perfect sound; how much more one who lodges in great calm and illumines the feelings of the multitude, who issues forth on touching circumstances and responds without thought, like the echo of a valley. Thus the patriarchs from of old who realized the wisdom that is natural and without a teacher — even a raised eyebrow or a blink, a scolding or a mocking laugh — none of it failed to point directly to the meaning of the coming from the west. How could one measure its form with the speech of discriminating feeling? Bodhidharma came west and established no letters, yet Caoxi has its Platform Sūtra, and the two lines and five houses, though they point directly to the one road above, all bend to the present time; whether in the hall or entering the room, showing the assembly or raising a point, their workings are like lightning and thunder. Whenever one of them let fall a phrase, it was sure to be compiled into a record. For the most part these are but the gateway; such were Dahui, Zhongfeng, and down to Chushi of our Ming — all of that kind. They borrow words to transmit the mind and see the Way through speech, speaking what is beyond speech. Now, more than two hundred years after Chushi, there appeared Chan Master Daguan, who rose abruptly to shake it with strength when the Chan school had already fallen. He obtained the wisdom without a teacher and held the diamond mind; his will to bear the Dharma-gate was like Li Ling’s bloody battle: though he brandished an empty fist, he still waved it at the setting sun. Though he did not trample the court and sweep the lair, his single thought of lone loyalty is not to be judged higher or lower by life and death against those who gnawed snow and swallowed felt. Truly a great, fierce, heroic man of the Dharma-ending age. Yet the master’s nature did not blend with worldly feeling: even in old age, seeing a guest, he never made a single bow. Though he never sat on the jeweled throne or raised the whisk, wherever his footprints reached covered half the world, and magistrates, laymen, those who turned their hearts at the sight of his shadow and bowed at the sight of his form, cannot be counted in myriads. Because he was thoroughly versed in his own nature, his words according to capacity were like a thousand-pound crossbow loosed: the target falls at the sound of the string. None of it was anything but pointing to the meaning of the coming from the west, uttered in accord with nature, never deliberately made into literature. A single spit and it was done; of what his disciples wrote down and kept, not one in ten. At first the master came and went between Jinsha and Qu’e, and with the Yu and Wang families his Dharma-bond was deepest. Layman Yu Runfu, whenever he obtained a scrap of the master’s writing, treasured it like a great jade disc. When the master traveled to Mount Kuang and lodged at the Changshan Lodge of the xiucai Xing Laici, many of his Dharma words remained with the Xing family. After the master’s transformation, Runfu asked Mr. Wang Zhonggao to gather them into one collection. I had long been sunk in the miasmic seas, and having completed the master’s final karmic business, I passed by the Eastern Chan at Jinsha; Runfu held out the master’s collection to me, bowed, and asked me to write its preface. I read his words three times, and sighed with a gasp: alas, in the Dharma-ending age to subdue the mind and uproot the very root of birth-and-death, like one man fighting ten thousand — I have seen this in the master alone. Beholding the strength, firmness, courage, and ferocity of his spirit, ever laid bare at the tip of his brush like a giant spirit wielding an axe — truly it is what is called doing battle with the demon of affliction, the demon of desire, and the demon of death, and being able in the end to leap beyond birth and death like casting off worn sandals; he may be called one who has fought and won merit. How then can what he spat forth be sought in letters, words, sounds, and forms? The Buddha said that desire is the root of birth-and-death; in all the master raised he always gave the point threefold attention, pricking the needle into the sore place, wanting directly to cut off the very root of life. This alone can serve as the golden scalpel — what need had he of gate-and-court establishments? Formerly Juefan of the Chan school, whose wondrous awakening was peerless, called what he wrote, in language and rules, “literary Chan,” and named it so himself. Therefore I title this the Collection of Old Man Zibai; it does not fall into the common measure. Readers should possess the diamond true eye and see it beyond the words; then more than half will be understood.
Preface to the Complete Works of Old Man Yunqi

Words carry the Way; writing conveys the principle. Of the speech that governs the world, even the sages’ classics are all called literature; only the Buddha’s words are not so, because of the difference between the worldly and the world-transcending, between feeling and beyond feeling. What the Buddha spoke he sealed with the seal of true marks, sealing all dharmas; all his words return to the true mark. This is what is meant by the path of speech being cut off and the sphere of mental activity being extinguished, so that it cannot be conceived or discussed. To seek it in literature is like holding ice and seeking fire. Not only the Buddha’s sūtras: even the coarse words and fine speech of the patriarchs from of old all return to the supreme first principle; how much more one who is rooted in letters yet transcends feeling. I have read the collection of Great Master Yunqi, and thrice over I sighed. The master started out as a Confucian and left the household life in middle age, single-mindedly investigating the one matter of the Buddha before his appearance and the patriarch before his coming west. He visited all quarters and had his awakening; then he hung up his gourd and hat, hid his traces at Yunqi, and nourished himself in quiet, knowing he had no intent toward the world — how much less toward literature. After long silence his voice and light shone out alone, and those who came asking the Way, black-robed and white-robed, at first filled his threshold, then stood like a forest, and at last gathered like clouds and mist, all with requests. Because what the master had attained was hidden and secret, and what he dwelt in was ordinary, in responding to capacities and meeting things he had no gate or court, no walled city, no cliffs of strangeness; he was like a mirror reflecting things, responding to the fair and the ugly alike. Therefore he passed no judgments and made no reproofs, but let each follow his own heart; so those who came were like mosquitoes drinking from the sea, each satisfied according to his measure. When his disciples recorded his words, they called it literature. Alas, could this exhaust the Master? In my youth I attended lecture halls and heard speakers discourse on the wonder of the Buddha’s responding to capacities, and did not know what they meant. In old age, reading the Diamond Prajñā — how the disciples, having returned from the Buddha’s begging rounds, ate, washed their feet, spread the seat, and sat down, and Śubhūti suddenly sighed and called the World-Honored One rare — I suddenly felt as if waking from a great dream. Thus one knows that the World-Honored One, living in the world and dealing with people, for the first twenty years had no one who knew what he was about, and only today did Śubhūti glimpse it. So too one knows Confucius’s sigh that none understood him: even Yan Hui, his foremost disciple, could only say that he looked up to it and bored into it, and in the end could not enter. How then can the words recorded by the various disciples exhaust Confucius? Alas, the sage’s influence in the world — how could ordinary men fully know it? Truly writing is the dregs. Yet the words of the Chan gate that carry the Way, apart from the Buddha’s sūtras and the patriarchs’ transmission-lamp records that point directly to the one road above — their words especially are greatly at variance and close to no human feeling, and so many gaze at the ocean. Even teachers of letters who recount the Buddha-patriarchs’ Way are drowned in feeling, and their readers are like willow catkins stuck in mud. To seek one level and solid and easily understood, direct and fully reasoned, like the moon shining on a hundred rivers, reflecting the clear and the muddy alike, so that those who can receive it are like men drinking sweet dew, with no illness unhealed — one who is thus next to the Buddha-patriarchs I have seen in the writings of Yunqi. Some critics say the master was a venerable teacher and elder scholar; I have always called him the Duke of Zhou and Confucius of the Dharma-gate. To look on the master as literature would be superfluous. Mr. Yan of Jiahe admired the master without having been personally instructed, and so carved his complete works to illumine later ages. Is he not too a loyal minister of this Way?
Preface to the Bequeathed Letters of Those Beyond the World

Of the worthy magistrates of Tang and Song who rested their minds in the joy of Chan, the records are in the books: men like Pei, Yang, Zhang, and Lü, at play in Dharma-joy with great elders like Huangbo and Dahui — all knocked at the gate and beat time, and none failed to reveal the one road above. It lies in a single word or half a phrase, like a probing pole or a shadow of grass. As for scraping away filth and polishing, knocking bone and striking marrow, using the native tongs and hammer to smelt the habit-energies — the giver is not at ease and the receiver truly finds it hard; hence such cases are rarely seen. In the late spring of the dingsi year, Feng Yanling of Zixuan saw me off in a boat at Wumen. The bequeathed letters of the two great elders Daguan and Lianchi, received by his grandfather the Hanlin Academician Kaizhi, are all in their own hands — not only urging the Dharma-gate and the bearing of the great matter, but in applying medicine to the illness, like Bian Que’s healing, seeing through to the lungs and liver, and the prescriptions they compounded are not merely for piercing the vital region and raising the disabled from their sickbeds. Passed down in the family, let sons and grandsons treasure them; they should be the wisdom-life, and not merely a treasure of ink and the moisture of a hand.
Preface to the Definitive Words of Great Master Yunqi

The Definitive Words are the direct pointing to the one mind, the fully explicit teaching. Our Buddha appeared in the world especially to open and show the one mind to living beings, causing them to awaken and enter it, pervading all dharmas without remainder. From shallow to deep, it begins with clinging to marks and breaking marks, and goes on to the mutual fusion of nature and marks; the setting up of the three vehicles is all a shielding, called the teaching that covers the mark, and none of it is explicit. Only when it clearly points out the one mind, with no remaining dharma, causing one to awaken suddenly right here, is it called definitive. Because delusion has depth and shallowness, the teaching is divided into sudden and gradual. At the very end, at the twirling of the flower, he pointed directly to the Way beyond words; Bodhidharma came west and transmitted this Way alone, calling it the sudden gate of the Chan school. Yet the purport of this sudden school is not Chan alone: in the various teachings, the explicit and the secret speak of it in more than one way. Because those who cling to the teachings are confused about the school, and those who cling to Chan slander the teachings, neither understands the Buddha’s definitive purport. Nor is it a matter of principle only: even the six perfections and the myriad practices that are set up are all practices that seek to clarify the one mind. Compared with Chan, only sudden and gradual differ; when they succeed, they are one. As for the single gate of the Pure Land and the cultivation of the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, this again gathers all three faculties and perfectly receives the sudden and the gradual, accomplishing it in one life — nothing surpasses it. The Buddha-patriarchs from of old have earnestly shown it, and not once only. Yet to my regret, students of the final age set their wills on empty mysticism, taking Chan as lofty and slighting the Pure Land and not practicing it. In a time of Dharma-ending, living beings’ defilement is heavy: how could everyone be called a sharp faculty? To deceive oneself so much and not measure one’s own vessel of virtue, only echoing others without a single practice — is that not to ruin oneself? Alas, the Chan school has long lacked a clear-eyed teacher, and none can set it right. As for the doctrinal students, their empty talk is shallow and mostly departs from actuality, so that not only is there no Chan, but the eye of the teachings is unclear — and it has never been worse than today. Great Master Yunqi awakened early to mind-only, and so earnestly upheld the Pure Land to save the ills of the final age. He built monasteries himself, taught his disciples by his own conduct, and day and night without remitting for nearly forty years; hence black-robed and white-robed throughout the seas believed and followed in great numbers. The master’s Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra draws it out almost entirely; and in his ordinary opening words and phrases, he mostly raises mind-only to unfold the purport of the Pure Land. The layman Zhu Xinkong, an inner-chamber disciple, recorded these words and named them Definitive. Truly they are a perfect mirror of the Chan school and a guide to the one mind, a golden scalpel that directly lances the film from the eyes of the final age. Lately, traveling as an official in Xingzhu, he entered the mountains to visit me and showed me the manuscript. Thrice over I read and thrice I sighed, and presumptuously wrote a turning phrase at the head of the volume.
The Dream-Journey Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twenty
Preface to The Pure Land Guide

The Pure Land Guide is a pointing of the cultivator to the Pure Land. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, in gathering and transforming living beings, has not one skillful means alone; and the essentials of his teaching from first to last comprise the two schools of nature and marks. Because the capacities differ in greatness, the teaching is set up as sudden and gradual, and at the last it is divided into the two gates of teachings and Chan: the teachings draw in and gather the three faculties, while Chan suddenly awakens the one mind. The whole canon and the seventeen hundred kōans have come down from of old. As for the one gate of the Pure Land, it covers all three faculties universally, and sudden and gradual alike enter it; no capacity is left ungathered. What is called crossing the three realms horizontally is the most supreme of Dharma-gates. Among the patriarchs from of old, there is not one awakened mind that did not take this as its final refuge. Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa earnestly praised it; that speakers took this as stooping to raise the middling and lowly shows they did not know the purport of the Pure Land. Truly, because the two kinds of retribution — dependent and proper — of all living beings in the ten directions, though they differ as superior and inferior, pure and defiled, are all conjured and transformed by the one mind, it is said that when the mind is pure the land is pure, and this is what is meant by the mind-only Pure Land. Thus the land is not outside the mind, and purity comes from the one mind. If one is not a person who has awakened the mind, how can one purify his land? Herein lies the reason why in the Chan house there is no one of the highest capacity who does not take refuge in the Pure Land. As for middling and lowly people, if they cultivate pure precepts, single-mindedly fix their thoughts, and keep contemplation continuous, at the end of life they will surely attain rebirth. Though there is the mark of coming and going, the marks and excellences of Amitābha and the jeweled trees and flower terraces are truly conjured and manifested by one’s own mind, like dream matters that come from nowhere outside. And as for foolish men and women who merely cultivate the ten good deeds, purely keep the five precepts, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name: at the end of life they too will surely attain rebirth. This is through the Buddha’s power of blessing and through the practitioner’s thought and imagining growing strong. By this superior imagining and that great vow, vow meets thought, and the mind of itself silently accords with the Buddha. Though the Pure Land has not yet appeared, the work of rebirth is already accomplished: it truly comes from the hidden response of one’s own mind, and is not outside either. As for the ten evil men, if at the end of life their karma prevails, and the bitter affairs of hell already appear before them, yet because they are pressed to the extreme and their wish to escape suffering is urgent, an extreme mind of suffering becomes the power of thought, and an utterly exhausted mind of remorse: at that very extreme point the whole body is transformed, a single thought accords with the Buddha, and so by the Buddha’s blessing power it appears at the thought — the mountain of knives becomes jeweled trees, the cauldron of fire becomes a lotus pool. Thus even these evil men attain rebirth. Yet this state of the Pure Land is truly the work of the whole mind’s transformation, and is not obtained from outside. Seen thus, of the three realms and all dharmas, not one dharma does not arise from the mind; of the lands pure and defiled, not one land does not appear from the mind. Therefore the one gate of the Pure Land, whether one is awakened or not, whether wise or foolish, is one that all who practice will surely attain: all is by one’s own mind. This, then, is the purport of the mind-only Pure Land, as clear as black and white. Because the Buddha’s essence is like space, when one’s own mind is empty and pure it becomes one with the Buddha in the dark; only by borrowing the adornment of a single thought of vow-power does the Pure Land suddenly appear, without depending on accumulated effort — this is the highest of the high, truly not something the shallow in wisdom and thin in faith can reach. Middling and lowly people, relying on the continuity of contemplation, are not swept away by the conditions of love and the habits of karma; though their faculties are somewhat inferior, their will is truly of the highest. Yet this cultivation is hard: the hard part is cutting off the root of love. For evil men rebirth is harder still. Though it is called carrying karma, it too is issued from the inner perfuming of good roots habituated in many past lives; though the root is coarse and inferior, a single thought of courage surpasses the highest. Compared with one who lays down the butcher’s knife and at once does the Buddha’s work, it is somewhat better. Yet such a case is one in ten thousand, not one; if people in the world must wait for this before seeking rebirth, they are mistaken. By my own observation, the root is neither great nor small: in the end it must be accomplished by a single thought directed upward. How then could this Dharma-gate have been set up for middling and lowly alone? General Xu of Ershi loved the cypress and rose through both letters and arms, discoursing on ritual and music and earnestly cultivating poetry and letters; in the leisure of discussing arms he kept his mind on the Pure Land. He is what is called one who uses compassion in warfare. He compiled the book Guide, taking the Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations as its doctrine, and drawing out the difficult questions to reveal the source of Buddha-recitation; next he cites the Pure Land school and Longshu and other sayings to show faith, vow, and right practice; next he lists the twenty-six persons from Master Yuan downward as actual evidence; and last he opens the exhortation to recite, unfolding the meaning of Buddha-recitation. Cause and effect are complete, and compared with the earlier Essentials of Cultivation, all is gathered here. Truly it may be called the guide to the Pure Land. I say that in this collection principle and phenomena are both cultivated, and cause and effect both revealed. If readers take this as their guide, then the land of wondrous joy will be bright before mind and eye without seeking it beyond a hundred thousand koṭi lands; and they will receive that supreme wondrous joy in the midst of their daily affairs, without waiting for the end of life and the transcendence of the spirit to call it actual proof. The benefit of this book is truly a compassionate ship on the sea of suffering and a torch of wisdom in the long night. How could it be small?
Preface to the Carving of the Ritual Norms of Yoga Buddhist Ceremonies

Our Buddha established his teaching to make plain the principle of birth and death, to penetrate the causes of the dark and the manifest, and to understand the feelings of spirits: no being is left unsaved, no suffering unplucked. Hence it is said that compassion takes as its object suffering living beings; without the extreme suffering of living beings, the vastness of compassion could not be seen. This Yoga teaching has its origin here. In Sanskrit, yoga means “correspondence,” that is, mind and object, outer and inner, being as one. The teaching has explicit and secret: the explicit directly points to the original mind-essence of living beings, causing them to awaken and so escape the bonds of birth and death; the secret is the mind-seal of all Buddhas, namely the divine spells, whose recitation confers blessing and causes all living beings to escape extreme suffering at once — all are ritual norms of saving living beings. The true words originally come from the anointment section; the reason for saving the dark and rescuing sunken spirits begins with the Venerable Ānanda, who sat in the forest by night and saw the ghost-king with the flaming face, and so initiated the teaching of food-offering. As for the spells over water and food, universally succoring beings as many as the sands of the Ganges, all came from the spirit-monks of India and flowed into China, transmitted as precedent. From the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, who proclaimed the secret words, it came gradually down to Emperor Wu of Liang: because Lady Xi of the Chi family had fallen into the body of a python and sought deliverance, the emperor asked the Monk Zhigong to gather the great virtuous monks and compile the Water and Land ritual text, so that the spirits of the three realms, dark and manifest, all without exception might fully express their feelings. Since then monks have followed one another in this, making it the Yoga Buddhist ceremony; it has been long in coming. In the time of our Sage Founder he fixed three categories — Chan, Doctrine, and Yoga — for ordaining monks: the Laṅkāvatāra, the Diamond, and the Buddha-patriarchs’ sūtras were used to test Chan and Doctrine; the flaming-mouth food-offering and the ferrying deliverance text were used to test Yoga. One who could master one of them was then permitted to be a monk. Today in the southern capital, Tianjie is Chan, Bao’en is Doctrine, and Nengren is Yoga, in observance of the national rule. Afterward vulgar custom gradually declined: by and large they broke the precepts and rules and treated it as a game, deeply losing the Tathāgata’s original intent of saving living beings. Even so, the purport of the text expresses the sincere feeling of the filial son and loving parent, and the secret true words proclaim the mind-seals of all Tathāgatas: a single verse turns hell into a pure land; a single phrase transforms the cauldron of boiling water into a lotus pool. When the sound of Dharma reaches, the offense is at once extinguished; when the bell’s sound arrives, the suffering at once stops. How could this be a small matter? To lose its purport is not only of no benefit but is to harm oneself; and none examines himself. A certain monk of Chu started out by means of Yoga and afterward studied with the great lecturers of Xuelang and the rest, hearing and learning the sūtras and treatises, and understood the Tathāgata’s intent of saving living beings. On returning, grieving at its abuses, he based his work on the Water and Land ritual text and compiled a ritual norm, adapting it to the times, dividing the sections and analyzing the principles so that each chapter is orderly. Thus those who have prayers to make may each according to their situation fulfill their sincerity, and monks and sons of Śākya may also unfold the compassionate mind and bare their sincere feelings without losing the root. This is a surpassing benefit for others. When the collection was complete the master passed away; his disciple so-and-so ably continued his will, wishing to print and circulate it to spread its transmission, so that those who perform Buddhist ceremonies may be without the fault of error and affront to the spirits, and may have the purport of earnest and pure sincerity; and so that the filial sons and loving parents of the world may each fulfill their minds and reach the spirits. Its merit is surely no shallow thing. He asked me for a preface to transmit it. I hold that whatever benefits living beings is a wondrous practice; therefore I have told him where Yoga comes from, so that men may know our Buddha’s bequeathed intent of saving living beings.
Preface to the Thousand Buddhas Repentance

Fundamentally, mind, Buddha, and living beings are three with no difference. Therefore the ignorance and affliction that living beings manifest and enact in daily life are precisely the fundamental actual wisdom of all Buddhas. This is what is meant by “living beings within the mind of the Buddha accomplish the Way at every moment, and Buddhas within the mind of living beings realize the truth thought after thought.” Thus living beings and Buddha are not separated by a hair. But because ignorance is deep and thick, one does not himself know or awaken, but pursues the false and loses the true, raising confusion and creating karma, long drowning in birth-and-death without being able to turn back. Truly this is pitiable. Our World-Honored One gave up his own Dharma-joy, manifested his body in the three realms, shared the troubles of the people, and saved and freed them. In the forty-nine years of his teaching, all the dharmas he spoke comprise manifold immeasurable skillful means, all of them tools for living beings to escape suffering. A bodhisattva’s cultivation is not beyond the two practices of benefiting self and benefiting others. The practice of benefiting others is vast; the practice of benefiting self is the most direct. Both are nothing but the understanding and penetration of one’s own mind, taken as the essential wonder. As for the practice of clarifying the mind, it is sudden or gradual: the sudden is nothing other than Chan investigation; the gradual is not beyond calm abiding and insight. As for these two practices, one of sharp faculty and keen wisdom, light in karma and thin in confusion, may enter directly; but middling and lowly people, heavy in the karma of birth-and-death accumulated over kalpas and deep in offense, even if they have the will to escape suffering, are obstructed by confusion and karma, and must accumulate the work of repentance to dissolve the obstruction of evil karma before they can enter. Know then that the one practice of repentance is the foremost Dharma-gate for cultivation and escape from suffering; no one of the three faculties, high, middling, or low, fails to begin from this. Even in the perfect-and-sudden Dharma-gate of the Huayan, where Samantabhadra is the guide of the Dharma-realm, of the ten vows he cultivates the first is necessarily to bow in reverence to all Buddhas, and the next in weight is to repent of karmic obstructions. The Śūraṅgama is the perfect school of explicit and secret, yet it must first establish the altar, bow to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and earnestly seek repentance; when repentance reaches the point where offense is extinguished and wisdom is born, the Buddhas appear in person, response and way meet, and one may be permitted to enter the Way. The Lotus is the great vehicle of the true mark, which Tiantai explained by a hundred realms and a thousand suchnesses in the perfect school of complete virtue and set out as calm abiding and insight; yet it must refine the repentance rites to practice true cultivation. In the Chan school, Chan Master Yongming personally realized the perfect fusion of the Dharma-realm, and yet he bowed to the Lotus repentance rite in season and never remitted in his life. Know then that the one gate of repentance is the foremost practice for entering the Way in the final age. I have heard that Śākyamuni, our original teacher, hearing the names of the fifty-three Buddhas, resolved his mind on cultivation and attained the fruit of Buddhahood; spreading it further, three thousand men each attained the supreme Way — hence they are called the three thousand Buddhas. Of those who have already become and not yet become Buddhas, their names and titles are fully set out in the canon; I am ashamed not to have explored the whole of their beginnings and causes. In recent times those who bow to the thousand Buddha-names have only the Buddha-names but no text of disclosure. The Liang repentance has been transmitted from of old; its text of declaring one’s feelings is complete, but the three thousand Buddha-names are not complete. I have often said that living beings of the final age are deep in offense and heavy in karma; it is like a man who breaks the law and takes refuge with a princely house and may thereby be pardoned. Beings in hell, pressed by suffering, call the Buddha’s name once and attain rebirth in the Pure Land — how much more those who bow in reverence here and now. Because the Buddhas, by their compassion of one substance, respond and bless, the essential of escaping suffering is nothing beyond the one gate of repentance. The Thousand Buddhas Repentance compiled by a certain man of Wumen takes the old text of the Liang dynasty as its basis, adds the Buddha-names not previously listed, gathers the received words of the teachings, and sets out the sincerity of disclosure; from first to last it is coherent, as if from one track — transmitting and not creating, with no private opinions. Looking at his mind of benefiting and ferrying, it is diligent indeed. If some criticize it, they have not probed the compiler’s mind, nor do they believe in their own minds. If one believes that one’s own mind is Buddha, and that it is screened by karmic filth as many as the sands of the Ganges, then to bow to Buddhas as many as the sands to dissolve it cannot be reckoned too many. The Dharma is fundamentally the mind: then what dharma is not a wondrous practice? Let no one grow weary because the Buddhas are many. The three thousand Buddhas were all guided by our original teacher; since the taste of Dharma is the same, and the reverence is one, the dharmakāya of all Buddhas enters my nature, and my nature is one with the Tathāgata. Like mirrors exchanging light, each takes in the other; truly we borrow the compassionate light of many Buddhas to dissolve the accumulated offenses of many lives. How much more than the blazing sun melting frost and dew: ten suns rising together burn the earth; the three thousand Buddhas appear, and the filth of offense is at once extinguished. This needs no seeking for proof; one must believe without doubt. Let readers only seek sincerely their own mind of escaping suffering, and believe in the greatness of the merit of bowing to the Buddhas and extinguishing offense, and need not reckon whether the compiler was right or not. I have written this preface to encourage true cultivators.
Preface to the Record of Joining Light on the Śūraṅgama

The Tathāgata, from first at the Deer Park to last at the Twin Sal Trees, in the forty-nine years of his teaching for one generation, did nothing but open and show the pointing to this mind. Because living beings’ confusion differs in thickness and their faculties in keenness, he set up the gradual stages of the three vehicles: by the ten good deeds to escape the suffering of the three evil paths, making clear the existent; by the truths and conditions to pull out the entanglements of birth-and-death in the three realms, making clear concentration; by the three contemplations to break the clinging to a fixed existence, making clear the middle. Yet though he set up many devices with skill, he must take the sudden realization of the one mind of the Dharma-realm as the ultimate standard. Hence he takes the great samādhi of the Śūraṅgama as the ultimate perfect destination. This is the one great matter for which our original teacher appeared in the world, the teaching of his whole life’s transformation. Know then that the setting up of the three contemplations is scattered through the five periods; the ocean of teachings is vast, and cultivators of the final age find its purport hard to penetrate. As for opening up the one mind of the Dharma-realm, gathering the teaching of one generation, unveiling the wondrous gate of the three contemplations, and revealing the purport of the one mind, nothing surpasses this single sūtra, the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama. Great indeed is the crown dharma, the hanging mirror that truly realizes the one mind suddenly. It gathers the vast exposition of the twelve divisions of the canon into ten fascicles of text; it sets out in detail the cause and effect of the ten dharma-realms within some sixty thousand words; it gathers the immeasurable ocean of practices into the wondrous gate of the three contemplations; and it perfects in the single samādhi of the Śūraṅgama the Buddhahood that is hard to accomplish through vast kalpas. It may be called the most simple and essential, the deepest and most profound of Dharma-gates. Since this sūtra entered China, its interpreters past and present number not less than several tens of houses. Though their views differ, each has his strength: some discipline the words but are blind to the common path; some prize the contemplation of principle but omit the words. In essence all of them want only to make the Buddha’s intent clear. But the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom leaves even the tenth ground gazing from the shore — how much more those who dwell in the outflows. Thus those who explore the teachings are like men drinking the sea: fish, dragons, mosquitoes, and gnats each exhaust their own measure; how could they exhaust the sea water? Yet a single drop already holds the taste of a hundred rivers. I have retired in age to Mount Kuang, shutting the pass and sitting withered. Siyi Shougong showed me the Record of Joining Light on the Śūraṅgama that he had composed, and asked me for a word to head it. I am ashamed that I am old, my eyes are dim, my wisdom lacks the mirror of discernment, and my thought does not reach the subtle; how could I draw out its deep mystery? Forcing myself to read it once, I saw how it lifts up the beginning and end, points out the veins, and guides the words as if the blade were moving through. With your expansive talent and unbridled brush, you shed the narrow paths and seem not to confine yourself to the carpenter’s square — like using a wedge to drive out a wedge, something not seen before. I think it will be convenient for the wise and the rounded capacity, but I fear the shallow in understanding will only add another film to their eyes. That lies with the reader, who must have a surpassing eye and gain it beyond the words. To awaken and enter by this is truly no small karmic cause. If a single word fits, it is like eating diamond; how then could its merit be conceived?
Preface to the Re-carving of the Sixth Patriarch’s Platform Sūtra

The World-Honored One taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, and then said he had not spoken a single word. At the last he twirled a flower, and Kāśyapa broke into a smile; and so there was the purport of a special transmission outside the teachings. In the western heaven twenty-eight patriarchs transmitted it one to another as the mind-seal. Bodhidharma came east, pointing directly to the one mind and establishing no letters. After six transmissions it reached Caoxi, and the robe and bowl ended there, because those who believed were many. The Sixth Patriarch received Huangmei’s mind-seal, awakening to “originally there is not a single thing,” and so made it his very bone. He opened the Dharma at Caoxi, teaching by not-teaching; his disciples, barking like dogs at a clod, compiled it and called it the Platform Sūtra. What it points out, though it be the one mind of prajñā with no dharma outside the mind, is what the mouth speaks — like the sound of a heavenly drum, like the echo of a hollow valley; how could it be an actual dharma? I, by grace, was beyond the mountains, and had the fortune to be a servant of the Sixth Patriarch; I have done some tidying of the fallen threads. I saw that of the several carvings of the sūtra many had been altered differently from one another — because clever gentlemen of later ages thought that Old Lu was originally a woodcutter who could not read a character, and wondered that what he said had no literary color, and so rashly changed it. Alas, the great sound is faint; the perfect writing is without writing; how much more when one unfolds the Way beyond words and borrows the tongue to proclaim it. The flowing water and the moving wind all proclaim the perfect sound — what writing is there in them? I chanced on an old edition and collated it, setting in order whatever in the record was uneven, and divided it into ten chapters, so as to match the title of sūtra more gracefully. It was carved in the mountains. It happened that the Great General Zhang Leqi, who had earlier opened a military headquarters in Yue, visited me in the mountains; I once gave him this sūtra. Ten years later the general returned to the forests; I passed by Qiantang, and he greeted me with joy as if born again. Speaking of this sūtra, he had already had it re-carved and circulated.
