Feeling that the general had the strength to bear the Dharma, I wrote this preface, to show that he is a Chan general, and as an encouragement to those who would bring forth the valor of seeing and hearing in this matter.
Preface to the Carving of the Platform Sūtra of the Dharma Treasure (Surviving Drafts from the Eastern Sea)

Someone says: our Buddha in forty-nine years, and at the last twirling a flower, declared that he had not spoken a single word; Bodhidharma came west, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha, establishing no letters, and this was called the single transmission. Is not this sūtra, then, letters? But such a one does not know that this matter is complete in everyone from the first, lacking not one dharma, establishing not one dharma. Since it is originally complete, then before the Buddha appeared in the world, every dust and every land was never not blazingly speaking; before the patriarch came west, every thing and every head was never not clearly pointing directly. Seen thus, the World-Honored One pointed directly all day long, and Bodhidharma taught the Dharma for nine years: how then is there inside the teachings or outside them, single transmission or double transmission? If a man suddenly sees his own mind, then whether one speaks or does not speak is all idle talk. This Platform Sūtra everyone knows came from Caoxi, but they do not know that Caoxi came from everyone’s own nature. Everyone knows the sūtra is letters, but they do not know that letters point directly to the mind. Outside the mind there is no dharma; outside the dharma there is no mind: one taste, equal, with not the least place of evasion. Alas for men, face to face they do not know. If they knew, they would truly believe without doubt, and originally there would be nothing to do. With nothing to do, what would it matter whether the Buddha-patriarchs appeared in the world or not, or spoke the Dharma or not? Thus this carving is a carving of the tracks of a bird in the air.
Preface to Words in Sleep on the Nyāyapraveśa

Fundamentally the whole Dharma-realm is unified in the one truth, clear and without any marks. Because of delusion it becomes form and mind; because of clinging it becomes self and dharma. Depending on others, false arisings of all kinds of pervasive imagination occur; views of existence and non-existence spring up across the way, and the perfect nature is obscured. Therefore our World-Honored One specially taught that the three realms are mind-only and all dharmas consciousness-only, to point directly at it; this is the ultimate doctrine, like a finger pointing at the moon. After the golden wheel hid its radiance and the jade-marked hair withdrew its color, within a hundred years wrong views again towered to heaven and nature and marks cut the ground into rival camps. Then there were the great arhats and masters such as Nāgārjuna and Dignāga who rose abruptly, pulled up the banners, and set up their treatises to crush the wrong and reveal the right, like water pouring from a high roof, to break them greatly. Later Śaṅkarasvāmin drew out the essential meaning of the various treatises and lifted up their main cords, naming it the Nyāyapraveśa, the Introduction to Logic. It verifies the wrong and the right and measures cause and effect; the three members interlace, and the one nature is perfect. It labors to make one leave error and cut off the false, and by this to make clear the model of the right doctrine. It may be called the key to the Dharma-realm and the divine tally of the true mark. Obtained, one may open the dark bolt; worn, one may withstand a great enemy. The empty throne of all dharmas — without this one cannot sit on it. How I sigh that east and west travel different roads and north and south different paths, and that the text is terse and the meaning deep, so that even a master craftsman knocks his forehead. Alas, men’s sighs of gazing at the ocean are old. My Dharma-brother Master Xuelang En was first to mount and rein in; Master Yunpu Yu followed in his footsteps. In the autumn of the gengyin year of Wanli the master hung his staff at Jimen. One evening he dreamed of seven golden men and ten silver men who told him he would meet Tian Fenjie, and that a man of office would annotate it. Awakening, he sought out the two treatises, the Jin and the Sheng, and probed them deeply with all his strength. Later he indeed met Master Jie’s new explanation, and meeting Mr. Yu Changru, who spurred his resolve, he leaned against the Twin Trees and conceived it; in two months he completed the exposition, exactly matching the dream, and named it Words in Sleep, marking the dream. Ah, the traveler records his years at Nalanda and questions Maitreya in Tuṣita: seen thus, was Master Yu without meaning? I came from the sea, and the master showed me his draft. Though I am not keen and cannot see through to the dark subtlety and pluck the fruit from the flower, yet as to saying that the dissimilar case has no place for what it establishes, that it blocks the actual own-mark and is mutually opposed, that it changes the case to explain right and wrong, and turns the thesis about to clarify the gathering — all these come from a deep, submerged surpassing; truly he has awakened from his dark sleep. Yet the true cause does not wait for the full lifting of the conditional and the complete; more than half the thought is already there. So the saying goes: it is easy for those who follow and cultivate, hard for those who first create. And to cross the pass by the crowing of a cock, to break the enemy by juggling balls — how easy is that to speak of? If readers by this make the doctrine clear, seeing the moon through the finger, wishing directly to see the great earth in a mote of dust and the great void through a crack, then as for the merit in the Dharma-realm, it is not merely a matter of arrangement and disposition. Even leaning on the armrest and propping on the tree, one will lift one’s head to heaven and sigh: how could that be compared to the moaning and the drunk?
Preface to the Diagram of the Twenty-Five Perfect Penetrations (Inscribed for Wang Hongtai, Chief Censor)

Vairocana takes the Dharma-realm as his body; thus every faculty and every dust pervades the whole Dharma-realm. In the body, raise a single pore: if it pervades, then every hair pervades. In the object, pick up a single mote of dust: if it pervades, then every mote pervades. In the mind, a single thought contains ten ages; past and present, kalpa and thought, are simultaneous: then every thought pervades. Thus there is not one dharma that is not a perfect penetration — how then could it be confined by the limits of faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and the seven elements? This alone is the realm of the great man of universal vision; how could one of inferior understanding enter it? Therefore at the Śūraṅgama assembly the World-Honored One specially borrowed the twenty-five great ones to open a single line of connection for everyone — much like pointing out Chang’an from within the Hanyuan Hall. It is but a bending to dandle the dull-rooted. Though every gate has its road and every place is open, yet seen with the true eye it cannot but make the eyes film and flowers grow. The layman folds them all together at once and rolls and unrolls at ease. If he lets them go, then mountains and rivers, the great earth, scale and shell, feather and fur, all alike radiate light. If he holds them fast, then the twenty-five men cannot but beg for their lives from the hand of layman Hongtai. Thus even Avalokiteśvara, so skilled at entering the perfect penetration, cannot but drag mud and water — and that too is a defeat. Examine it finely: after all, what breath remains? The clear-eyed will see for themselves.
Preface to the Carving of the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries

Vairocana takes the Dharma-realm as his body and the adornments of the Huayan as the realm of his reward. Because in the cause of former times he cultivated in accord with the mind of the Dharma-realm, it is called a treasury: this mind in living beings is called the storehouse consciousness; in the Buddha it is called the Tathāgata-garbha mind. Hence in the dependent fruit it is called the world of the Huayan treasury. “Treasury” means containing and gathering without remainder, like a royal treasury in which nothing is lacking and whose use is inexhaustible. Therefore a bodhisattva’s cultivation is called the inexhaustible treasury: taking the wondrous practice that is the mind itself as the Dharma-wealth of merit, filling the measure of the mind, it is called the practice of the inexhaustible treasury. This is the mind-essence of the Dharma-realm that the Huayan takes as its doctrine, adorned by wondrous practice, complete and full; hence it is called Buddha. As for the causal practices cultivated, there are the distinctions of the ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, and ten grounds. This chapter corresponds to the completion of the ten practices, about to proceed to the ten dedications; hence it cultivates this practice of the ten inexhaustible treasuries. Accumulating within the one mind, one then dedicates it to three places — living beings, bodhi, and actuality. One accumulates practices to form a treasury; the practices disperse and the fruit is accomplished; hence one proceeds to the Buddha-ground. Abiding and practice are like accumulating; dedication is like dispersing — what is called accumulating and being able to disperse, and by dispersing perfecting virtue. It is like a sage who diminishes what is superfluous to serve the world: a matter of flourishing governance. Hence it is said: being is taken as benefit; non-being is taken as use. Therefore our Buddha, the World-Honored One, uses the Dharma-treasury that exhausts the Dharma-realm to succor the living beings of his own nature, and by it adorns the fruit of reward that is mind-only. Consider the wondrous matter of the Huayan adornment — how could it be sought outside the mind? Only because living beings are narrow and selfish and cannot expand the measure of their own minds. I had shut the pass at the Tanhua Vihāra by Linghu; my disciple Guanheng came from afar to inquire after me, and seeing me reading this chapter, rejoiced, bowed, and praised it, saying, “Great is the wondrous practice that universally illumines the deluded quarters; truly it is like the sun of wisdom lighting up the heavy darkness.” He asked for a preface and had it carved separately. I delight in giving the Dharma, and wish that those who see and hear and rejoice may by this see the inexhaustible wondrous practice of their own minds. If they believe and hold it, then the Huayan adornment may be climbed step by step, and the fruit of Buddhahood realized thought after thought; and their narrow, selfish habits will turn into an inexhaustible treasury of merit. Would that not accomplish a great matter?
Preface to the Revival of the Seventh Patriarch’s Monastery on Mount Qingyuan

The Buddhadharma rests on the teaching of images, and the Chan Way is lodged in the patriarchs’ courts. Thus at the sight of a temple the Three Jewels are present before one; at the pointing to a monastery the lamp of wisdom flares. For the Way is made great by men, and affairs are made manifest through principle; therefore the ancestral seats of the patriarchs must not be allowed to vanish, any more than the blood-vessels of a human body may rest for a single breath. Can the noble man who bears the Way fail to keep them in mind? The first patriarch of the Chan school came west, pointing directly to the supreme one vehicle, causing men to become Buddha on the spot. This Way was transmitted six times to Caoxi, and Qingyuan and Nanyue were its very bones. The two men raised their standards and greatly flourished in Jiangxi and Hunan; beneath them the five lamps divided their flames, all taking the two elders as their fire-maker. This Way is bright as the sun and moon in mid-heaven, and though for a thousand years it has been obscured, it shines the more; thus one knows that this mountain is of the greatest weight for men’s minds and the ways of the world. In my youth I once paid reverence to the Seventh Patriarch, and saw that its monks were not apart from the vulgar and the temple lay in waste among brambles, with only the shrines of the worthies honored and sacrificed to within it. At that time I sighed with feeling: the gods serve the Buddha; the worthies serve heaven. Each honoring its own principle may be fitting, yet I feared the spirits were not at ease. I lingered and departed. Once, in conversation with Chan Master Zibai, I said that the Chan school is desolate because the source must be dammed, and that we should together open and channel it; the master greatly agreed. The master waited for me first at Mount Kuang. In the yiwei year, when I was fifty, I was censured for spreading the Dharma and banished beyond the mountains; and so I was able to dredge anew the source of Caoxi, as an omen of the revival of the Chan Way. After eight bitter years the patriarch’s court began to open; though the work was not complete, the mechanism of revival was already visible. On an autumn day of the xinhai year, Zou Kuangming of Anfu, whose courtesy name was Ziyin, resolved to restore Qingyuan, and brought a letter from the Supervising Secretary Zou as an introduction, saying that Ziyin was a loyal minister of the Seventh Patriarch. I heard it and leapt up, and first instructed him that settling the shrine of the spirits was the first principle. At that time the conditions had not met, and it was laid aside. In the guichou year I went to the Southern Marchmount to keep my appointment with Zeng Yibu of Jinjian; he wished to revive it but his strength was insufficient. In the bingchen year I mourned Zibai and made a journey to Wu and Yue; reaching Shuangjing, I saw the Chan Way greatly revived and many investigating it. I sighed, “This is the Caoxi line flowing out anew.” In the summer of the dingsi year I returned to Mount Kuang to make plans for rest in old age, and saw the Donglin Lotus Society reopened and the Shimen Chan session concluded. I rejoiced greatly; within three days the letter from the Supervising Secretary also arrived, saying that Qingyuan was being greatly repaired and hoping for a word of guidance. For this was Ziyin’s long-cherished wish, continuing my own original vow. The shrine was already settled, and the first to give as benefactors, wishing to accomplish the main Buddha, were Liu Jinqing, Zhang Shouchang, and Guo Lingxi. I then sighed with great spirit: the Sixth Patriarch said, “The leaf falls and returns to the root.” The Chan Way, from the single vein of Caoxi, began at Qingyuan; and the patriarchs of the transmission-lamp record gradually declined after Zhongfeng, and in the early years of our dynasty were rarely seen. Since I dredged Caoxi, within a few years this Way revived again between Tianmu and Shuangjing in Yue, and is now being drawn back to Shimen on Mount Kuang, just as Qingyuan greatly flourishes; after a thousand years we see this day again — is this not an answer to the prophecy of the leaf returning to the root? In former times of flourishing, none flourished more than Mazu in Jiangxi; now revival is seen again at Qingyuan. Thus one knows that the turning of the Way’s fortune flows with the transformations of nature. Truly, I think, the eighty-one men who will come forth together beneath the colt are to be hoped for from today. In this task the merit of the benefactors is borne by many and does not wait on my words. Therefore I have specially recounted the reasons for the rise and decline of the Chan Way to tell my comrades: it lies not in adorning Buddha-lands but in making bright the Buddha-lamp, to aid the days of Yao and Shun, and to share with the people the transformation of non-doing. How could it be spoken of in the same breath as the ordinary building of a temple or the founding of a hall as a Buddhist work? The tenth day of midsummer, the forty-fifth year of Wanli.
Preface to the Continuation of the Dharma Lineage of Huayue Temple

Bodhidharma came west, single transmission and direct pointing, mind sealing mind; those of wondrous awakening are the very-boned sons and grandsons. Originally there were no names. When it had been transmitted six times to Caoxi, and beneath that to Nanyue and Qingyuan, the Way divided into two lines; because each followed its own transmission, they too were not rigid. When the five houses each set up their own house, they were called the such-and-such house; but “house” only means the doctrine they established, to let men know where to turn, and not that a borrowed name was the vein of the Way. Afterward the Chan groves declined day by day, teachers passed things mouth to ear, and in the monasteries throughout the world, whoever was the founding patriarch, if he originally belonged to some house, was each honored as the first ancestor. Because of the five families the Linji Way alone spread through the world, most temples within the seas acclaimed it. This is but conventional truth in circulation, and it has been long in coming. Huayao Temple in Hengzhou originally came from Linji, and takes the monk who reopened the mountain, Shaoxiu, as its first ancestor, establishing twenty characters: Shaozong Xipu Dao, Zhengke Sitong Xuan, Yuanming Zhenxing Hai, Fayang Fu Chong Yuan. These are now exhausted. It happened that I came to lodge at Linghu and was about to travel east; the temple’s abbot and the assembly burned incense and bowed, asking me to establish their lineage. I made no objection, and taking the character yuan as the beginning, continued forty more characters, with this verse: From Caoxi the source was dredged; the lamp was passed down from Nanyue. Widely open the principle of purity; wondrously awaken to the patriarchs’ Chan. Suddenly understand the purport of mind-only; take refuge in the exposition of actual wisdom. The subtle, secret meaning of the coming from the west: blessing and wisdom without bound. Is this enough to continue the school’s wind? I use a borrowed name only to speak of the true mark, so that the original source may not be obscured. Let the sons and grandsons of later ages revere and not neglect it.
Preface to the Building of the Portrait Hall of the Patriarchs at the Revived Tiantai Temple on the Southern Marchmount

In the past the great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai recited the Lotus Sūtra and saw with his own eyes the assembly on Vulture Peak, still seated and not yet dispersed. He sought verification from the great Master Si of Nanyue, who said, “This is the Lotus samādhi.” Thereupon Zhiyi composed the wondrous gate of calm abiding and insight. An Indian master said that it was largely the same in purport as the Śūraṅgama Sūtra of India. Hearing it, the master gazed west and bowed day and night for nineteen years, wishing to see this sūtra. The present Tiantai Temple on the Southern Marchmount is the place where the great Master Zhiyi bowed to the sūtra; more than a thousand years have passed and the bowing platform still stands. Zeng Jinjian of the Ministry of Rites wished to carve the Śūraṅgama Sūtra in stone on the platform, to fulfill Zhiyi’s aspiration; the great vow was not accomplished. This is one karmic thread of Tiantai. I and Master Zeng were Dharma-friends, and long planned to end our years together on the Southern Marchmount. In the winter of the guichou year, his eldest son Fuyao brought his father’s letter and welcomed me to the east of the lake. I came at his bidding, and saw eighty-eight scrolls of the patriarchs’ portraits of the Way. These were commissioned by Chan Master Daguan, who had his Danyang disciple He Zhiren engage the famous brush of the gentleman Ding Nanyu. There were three halls: two sets were placed at Wutai and Emei, and this one was specially for the Southern Marchmount. It had long been kept by the He family. In the gengxu year, when Master Zeng traveled to the southern sea, he passed by Qu’e, and Mr. He asked him to take them home to the Southern Marchmount; but since there was no place in the mountains to put them, they remained east of the lake. There I unrolled and did reverence to the countenances of the Way, as if entering the chambers of the patriarchs. At once I resolved to build a portrait hall to enshrine them, and wrote a subscription appeal. The Chief Minister Cai Huaiting took the lead in person, but the vow was in the end not accomplished. In the bingchen year I traveled east to Wu and Yue, and afterward retired in old age to Mount Kuang. Six years later, in the xinmao year, my disciple Ruyi wrote that Tiantai had been restored and that he wished to revive it. It happened that Master Zeng’s eldest son, in obedience to his father’s dying command, was sending the patriarchs’ portraits into Tiantai for offering, together with my earlier appeal. I heard it and said with joy, “This is my last unfinished vow.” Alas, Dharma-conditions and the times make each other appear or hide; it is all fortune. The Buddha said that all dharmas are unified in the one mind; hence there are the two schools of nature and marks, rooted in a single accord. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, nature and marks stood horn to horn and divided the river to drink apart — this is old. Not to speak of India: in these lands the teachings come from Tiantai, which set out the three contemplations to clarify the one mind; Chan comes from the twirling of the flower, and after twenty-eight transmissions Bodhidharma came east as the first patriarch. The five houses set up their lines, each established its house, and they reviled one another, and by and large none could unify them. Now the portraits of all the patriarchs are gathered here, and the single Śūraṅgama Sūtra unifies teachings and Chan and brings them home to the one mind. This is the ultimate destination of the two schools: without being expected to meet, they meet of themselves. Dwelling east of the lake, I wished to enshrine the patriarchs but my vow was not fulfilled; so I composed the Comprehensive Discussion of the Śūraṅgama to reveal the one road above of the Buddha-patriarchs and to bring the three contemplations and the one mind into accord, thus giving free course to Zhiyi’s unfulfilled aspiration. Now Ruyi has obtained that place and enshrines the patriarchs within it; it not only completes my unfinished karmic thread but fulfills Zhiyi’s unfinished mind. How fortunate! Ruyi, if you can indeed exhaust your strength and forget yourself in this work, then though I am old, I can still sit on the bowing stone and expound the Śūraṅgama, acting as my broad and long tongue, so that a thousand peaks nod, the myriad forms lower their brows, space is struck dumb, and the rival banners all surrender. The great Master Zhiyi will surely prick up his ears in the stillness and light, and as his habit-energy surges he will dance in the ocean of the lotus treasury, coughing and snapping his fingers together with all the patriarchs. The subscription appeal I wrote before; so I recount only the karmic thread of the portraits, and the beginning and end of Ruyi’s building, to tell the benefactors and serve as a guide for the vanguard. This is the preface.
Preface to the Dharma Lineage of Jiaoshan

The Dharma lineages of the patriarchs recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp were transmitted only by mind-seal; originally a borrowed name was not taken as an actual dharma. Alas, the Chan Way has declined and its true source grown dim. From Bodhidharma’s coming west it was transmitted six times to Caoxi, establishing not a single dharma. When the five houses divided, it was because their gate-and-court arrangements differed, while their doctrines were not different. Through Song and Yuan the lamps continued one to another, and in the early years of our Ming the old models still survived; afterward the lineages of the school were as nothing, because there was no clear-eyed master. The temples within the seas are like clouds, and monks everywhere say they come from such-and-such a house; but they take only the character-lineage as orthodox, and one never hears of mind sealing mind. Seen thus, it is greatly to be lamented. The whole world is so; how much more a single region. Moreover the Buddha’s rule had the four classes leave household life and share the single surname Shi, like many streams entering the sea. Now if one traces the true transmission of the five houses: the Fayan line early entered Korea; Weiyang fell silent; Yunmen still survived in Song, and Caodong was the sole specialty of Shaolin. Today the monasteries of the world mostly claim the Linji lineage, and that one line flourishes. As for the true branches and side shoots, they can no longer be traced; each man sets himself up, like the kingly order losing its bonds while usurpers rise across the way. The number of those who lose their way is great; who can set it right? A certain Chan man of Jiaoshan at Jingkou came from afar to Mount Kuang, asking for a lineage character-line. He said that the ten hermitages of this mountain originally descend from the first ancestor, Chan Master Juechu Zuxin, a side branch of Linji, the so-called Bodhisattva Jia; but the sons and grandsons of recent times are all confused about their source. The Chan man grieved over it, and so examined the order of the ten hermitages and compiled a genealogy, rectifying names and positions to hand down to later descendants. Though it is a borrowed name, this too is establishing a teaching through names; perhaps by this the distinctions of high and low among monks may be preserved, and none dare overstep, so that they do not come to despise human bonds and offend righteousness. This above all can preserve our sons and grandsons; it is the meaning of keeping the sheep, and brings benefit. Their first sixteen transmissions are exhausted; so I continue thirty-two more characters, following conventional truth. If one takes this as the school itself, then Linji would have to say that its own treasury of the true Dharma-eye was long ago extinguished.
Postface to the Poems of Dinghu Mountain

The White Cloud Temple on Dinghu Mountain is of long standing. In the days when the Caoxi Dharma-way flourished, those who came forth from its gate all saw the mind-seal clearly and were models for gods and men. Chan Master Zhichang was one who attended with towel and pitcher alongside the elders of Qingyuan and Nanyue. The two elders transformed their regions, and Master Chang withdrew to this mountain and ended his days there. The Brahma banner still stands, and his sacred remains are kept here; truly he was the Chao Fu and Xu You of the Dharma-gate. When I was young and able to read, I knew the story of the wilds of Cangwu and of riding the dragon at Dinghu, and took it as a fine tale invented by lovers of the marvelous to praise men of high ascent. In the spring of the bingshen year I was graciously banished to Leiyang; two years later, in the wuxu year, I put on cap and sash and taught the Dharma in the field of spears and halberds at Qingmen in Wuyang. At that time my disciple Bao Gui, whose courtesy name was Benjing, filled the first seat. When the assembly ended he bowed and said he would hide himself on Dinghu. I was astonished and delighted beyond measure and questioned him about the remains there; he said they had long been ruined. Governor Wang, when he was prefect of Duanzhou, had ordered the elders to repair them, and now they had fallen again. So I strongly urged Master Gui to dwell there, and enjoined him to still his mind, fix his will, and spend his whole life there; if he did so, I would retire in old age there too. Master Gui took my words, forgot himself in the work of the mind, and took Master Chang as his charge; with bitter heart and toil of body, enduring what could not be borne, another three years passed. In the gengzi year I entered the mountain and bowed at Master Chang’s stupa, and then made the first plans for Master Gui, fixing the scale, the essential being to settle the spirits and have enough for cultivation. Within a year the Three Jewels were rebuilt, the Buddha images adorned, and all shone with light. I rejoiced and praised it. On an autumn day of the guimao year I went to Caoxi, and made a pact with him for the summer retreat at Dinghu the next year. In the last month of spring of the jiachen year I left the mountains to visit the governor-general, and was about to make the journey to Leiyang; illness came upon me and I could not set out, so I moored my boat by the river bank, hoping to escape the heat in the mountains and go when autumn came. Within days I received the censor’s summons and dared not linger; I gazed with disappointment at the cloud mountains within my brows and could not go once. Was this not karma? That I could not go even once — from this one may see that to dwell permanently on this mountain is a fortune of coolness beyond a myriad kalpas of gods and men. When my illness was somewhat better I set out on the road; Master Gui comforted me from time to time in the boat. I was ashamed to be laughed at by the mountain spirits, and could not bear to part; so I wrote five poems and entrusted them to him in farewell, and sent greetings to Master Chang. Another day, if Heaven grants the condition, I shall raise a stupa for you amid the wild brambles and thickets.
Preface to the Gazetteer of Jingshan

The famous mountains and great rivers within the realm are recorded in full in the geographical books. When the Buddhadharma entered China, the jeweled palaces and Brahma temples all lodged their traces in famous mountains and celebrated places, spread everywhere like stars. This is the hidden flowing of the vein of the Way, by no means to be compared with those who seek out the strange and admire the marvelous. The ancients called local gazetteers unorthodox histories; the gazetteer of a Buddhist temple is a monastic history. Now Shuangjing is the most celebrated wonder of the southeast. From the founding of the mountain by Guoyi it was called a Dharma-seat. Its mountain runs eastward from Kunlun and towers among the Five Marchmounts; the southern range comes from Heng and Xiang, winding several thousand li, rising straight at Huangshan and the White Peak, and gushing up in two eyes that melt and congeal into this mountain, concentrating its numinous excellence. Thus the temple was first founded in a certain year of the Tang, and passed through Song, Yuan, and our Ming — a thousand years up and down, in which eighty-one men in succession were leaders of the Dharma-gate. Had the mountain’s congealed essence not been thick, how could it have endured so long? In the early years of our dynasty it still lacked no men. In the last hundred years the Dharma-banner has toppled and the monks are few. About the jichou year of Wanli, Chan Master Daguan rose abruptly and set up the red banner of the school; at that time he initiated the carving of the fangce canon, first proposed at Wutai, where monks who went to request it wore their feet to calluses over several thousand li. Before long it was moved to the Jizhao hermitage on the mountain, and the halls were likewise renewed because of it; this was the turning again of the Dharma-wheel. Shortly after, the Hanlin Academician Feng again proposed to open the ancient Huacheng as a place for storing the blocks. The provincial authorities and the great officers of the day were deeply minded to restore it. When Master Da entered nirvāṇa, his disciple Master Danju Kai was able to bear his work, and Master Da in the end obtained a stupa beneath Pengtuan Peak, in the same line as Dahui. Was this a small karmic cause? Yet those who dwelt on this mountain in former times, though skilled at raising the school’s vehicle, drew only a drop from the ocean of Dharma. Now the whole Tathāgata-garbha ocean is gathered and poured into it, as the complete lifting of the Dharma-gate; the karmic cause surpasses the past by ten thousandfold. Huang Zhenfu said that when Xiao He entered the passes, he took not a hair of the women, children, jade, and silk, but gathered only the maps and registers, and in the end made Han king by it. Now the great canon is the map and register of the Dharma-realm: to gather it all here and expand the Dharma-king’s territory must greatly depend on this. Had this mountain’s congealed energy not been broad and thick, how could it bear so heavy a Dharma? Alas, it is easy for those who follow and cultivate, hard for those who first create. For the great work of the present revival of the Dharma-gate, unless the maps and registers are orderly, how will later ages examine it? Therefore the gazetteer of Jingshan had to be made, and not merely to record its wonders. So I have recompiled it for ease of consultation, and have specially written this preface.
Preface to the Wondrous Bright Hall of the Bodhi Hermitage

I sat at the Bodhi Hermitage, where a new abbot’s chamber had been built; the host asked for a name for the hall, and I inscribed it “Wondrous Bright.” The assembly asked for instruction. The old man’s intent takes the two phrases from the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, “the nature’s awakening is wondrously bright” and “the original awakening is bright and wondrous.” Because Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇī, hearing that the faculties, body, and world before him were each pure and spontaneous, raised the doubt: if all is pure and spontaneous, how do the mountains, rivers, and great earth and all conditioned dharmas suddenly arise? He thought that within a pure realm no such things should be permitted to arise. The World-Honored One, come to this point, truly found it hard to open his mouth; so he took the two phrases he ordinarily taught — “the nature’s awakening is wondrously bright” and “the original awakening is bright and wondrous” — and questioned him with the double meaning. The first phrase does not belong to delusion or awakening: the natural wondrous nature is originally numinous of itself, hence “the nature’s awakening is wondrously bright.” The second phrase is what is cultivated and attained without being lost amid delusion, hence “the original awakening is bright and wondrous”; it means that though now attained by cultivation, it is not obtained from outside, but is the awakening each person originally has. The Buddha questioned him with these two phrases, intending to use the crucial point of delusion and awakening to open him up. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇī indeed took the phrase “the original awakening is bright and wondrous” as the attainment, thinking that the nature’s awakening is originally numinous and wondrous, and bright without need of further brightening; but then there is only the brightness that can brighten, and no awakening that is brightened. His intent was that there should be an awakening that is brightened, which alone would be apt. He did not know that the moment there is an awakening that is brightened, the endless false dharmas of the opposition between subject and object arise from this. Because all living beings, in birth and death, death and birth, have every dharma arise from within the pure realm by a single thought forcibly raised without cause, wishing to brighten the awakening — and with brightness and awakening, subject and object stand clearly — therefore he next unfolded the false dharmas of subject and object, clear and distinct, thus probing deeply the source of the Dharma-nature. This hermitage is named Bodhi; in Sanskrit, bodhi means awakening. Because everyone knows the Buddha attained by cultivation but not the Buddha originally possessed, the old man’s intent is true cultivation: one must first awaken to the undeluded nature. Then though one cultivates the myriad practices, one does not fall into ordinary feeling, and so, without leaving this very place, one suddenly realizes bodhi. The first mind must awaken to the wondrous brightness. Therefore I name the hall so.
Preface to the Golden Lotus Society at the Guanlai Rock on Mount Wutai

Qingliang is the golden realm, where Mañjuśrī with his ten thousand attendants ever dwells; it is the dwelling of the bodhisattva in the northeast as recorded in the Avataṃsaka. Since the mountain was opened in the Han, China has taken refuge there as a Pure Land among men; those who go back and forth each year number in the hundreds of thousands and millions. Arriving, they tread ice and snow and never weary of the toil. Had true compassion not received them, how could it be that for two thousand years not a single day has been empty? The mountain’s scenery is surpassing: rare flowers and strange grasses bloom here and there in profusion, like the seven treasures spread over the ground; golden lotuses burst forth, wondrous and lovely, each fresh against the other — truly not of this dusty world. Men of lofty character who lodge in truth and nourish the Way fill the valleys; temples are spread like stars, bells and drums hear one another, and the sound of Brahma is performed, together with the sighing of pines and the sound of springs, as a broad and long tongue, day and night without pause. Is this not a single true Pure Land among men? On the mountain there are monasteries everywhere, but formerly none was named a society; societies began with the Universal Gate and Qixian. Lately the host of the Jing Pavilion at the Guanlai Rock has formed a Golden Lotus Society, which was founded by the magistrate Mr. Li. His name was Maochun, a man of Qixian in Henan. At first his mother dreamed that three monks entered the room; she scolded them, and two at once left, only one not going, who said, “I am a monk of Wutai and wish only to form a bond.” That night she gave birth to him. He was born crying greatly; his mother would call to him, “You have a monk’s nature”; even at seven he still often cried and was unhappy, and whenever his mother called him a monk he stopped. Growing up, he asked his mother, and she told him of the dream; afterward he passed the jinshi examination in the guiwei year and rose to be military commissioner of Yanping. Traveling at Loufan, he suddenly recalled the past and said, “Master Yuan was born here and formed the Lotus Society at Mount Kuang; why have I forgotten my old home?” So he vowed to form a Golden Lotus Society at Wutai. First hearing of the Great Master Miaofeng, he went to take refuge and built a quiet room at Lingjiu to lodge there. Afterward, wishing to make a Buddha-recitation society himself, he heard the Wutai monk Huanzhu speak of the surpassing places of Mount Tai and say that the host of Guanlai Rock, Jingting, practiced austerities; so he turned his heart to him and donated funds for him to build the Lotus Society, in emulation of the precedent at Mount Kuang, cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. I had a journey to Shuangjing, and Master Jing sent a special messenger into the mountains to ask me for an account of the matter. I sighed deeply: the vast universe, the drifting waves — those who go and do not return are many; how many know their place of refuge? The Pure Land is the other shore of the sea of suffering. As for those who hold the boat and raise sail, cutting the stream and crossing over, up and down a thousand years and more — how many are they? Master Yuan founded the Lotus Society at Mount Kuang, and those gathered in succession were about a hundred and twenty-three, of whom eighteen worthies are singled out, appearing in the West and receiving one another in turn. This is the first surpassing matter since the Dharma came east. Mr. Li has risen a hundred generations later, rousing himself from the turbid and evil, and wading across to the land of joy. Had he not the root-strength of past lives and manifested the body of a magistrate, how could he have done this? I know that the rise of this society will carry him with the ten thousand attendants in the compassionate ship, raising sail on the calm stream to ascend straight to the other shore — how then could they be reckoned in hundreds or tens? It lies in the boatman’s long grip on the helm, sparing no strength. (A concluding passage of the source is missing here.)
Preface to the Karmic Cause of the Restoration of Tiansheng Temple in Huzhou

The Avataṃsaka says that the buddha-lands of the ten directions are like the mesh of Indra’s net hung in space: those forming, those abiding, those decaying, those empty are all of one and the same horizon. All Buddhas, with the ocean-assemblies of bodhisattvas, teach the Dharma and transform living beings; all kinds of spiritual powers and wondrous functions fill every place at once, like the intertwining light of the net’s pearls, each distinct and unimpeded. And all living beings, within the light of the wisdom-mind of all Buddhas, adorn buddha-lands, tame living beings, and commit the ten evils and five heinous acts, wandering the three realms and six paths in good and evil karma, and do not know it themselves. Hence it is said that the Buddha’s realm is inconceivable and the mental courses of living beings are inconceivable. Now at Tiansheng Temple in Huzhou this is fully seen. At the end of the year jiawu, the temple monk Zuding visited me at the Cishi Pavilion in the capital, and chanced to speak of the temple’s karmic history. He said its hall is vast, like emptiness; its adornments are dense and intricate, bracket on bracket clustered, tiles overlapping like a net. Of its makers, this is the first inconceivable thing. It was first founded in the Tang, its origins no longer traceable; it passed through Song and Yuan and to the present, nearly a thousand years. Yet along all the beams and among the brackets there is not the least dust; hence it is called the Dustless Hall. This is the second inconceivable thing. On its two pillars and exposed columns, dragons are carved of wood: heads and horns, whiskers and brows, claws and teeth as if flying, like living dragons, ascending and descending left and right. Once they sported in the pond; a temple monk saw them and scolded them, and the dragons returned to the hall and coiled crosswise, left and right. Hence it is also called the Hall of the Cross-Coiled Dragons. This is the third inconceivable thing. Its walls are more than two zhang across, formerly whitewashed; long ago Zhao Mengfu read there and was pleased with it, and on the two walls painted two panels of mist and rain over the Xiao and Xiang, while his wife Lady Guan painted a single panel of bamboo. In the several hundred years before this, were there no wondrous brushes of painting? Yet it had to wait for Ziang and his wife to touch and dye it — was this to mark the rise and fall of the present? This is the fourth inconceivable thing. The Buddha in the hall was built up in its form from copper coins: this surely was the mind of those who made it, and is inconceivable. In the Jiajing period of the Ming someone destroyed the Buddha, stripping sinew and breaking bone, tearing apart the net of flesh of coins, splitting the arhats and boiling them to eat. That man in the end felt an iron comb scratching his itch, until the skin and flesh of his whole body came away to the bone, and he died under punishment. Yet the world fears the spirits and reveres the Buddha: even madmen and drunkards still shudder and turn to him. But such a one as this minced him and was glad. This again was the mind of the destroyer, inconceivable. Hence today the temple is desolate and rough, as empty as if abandoned. The Grand Minister Lu Wutai passed by and sighed, and with the prefectural magistrates Xu Jing’an, Shen Jishan, and Feng Jiuqu resolved to restore it, appointing the bhikṣu Zuding to lead. At the beginning of the building, they sought a basis for the founding; that night a great wind broke an old mulberry tree, and when it was dug up in the morning, beneath the roots they found an ancient broken stele, which they read: it was from the Zhonghe period of the Tang, when the layman Wu Yan gave up his dwelling as a temple, its ground ninety-three mu in extent, and the prefect Wang petitioned for the plaque name Jingqing Chan Temple. Tiansheng was rebuilt in the Song and named for its year; without this none would know its source. Thus wood and stone, though without feeling, responded to the condition and accomplished the matter: feeling and non-feeling meet in response and way, like clear water reflecting the moon — this is again greatly inconceivable. Seen thus, the forming, abiding, decaying, and emptying of buddha-lands is already inconceivable; and as for the people, one may know the givers, the makers, the accomplishers, the abiders, the adorner, and the destroyer — their good and evil mental courses all different. Now in one morning they blaze forth together within the great light of the wisdom of all Buddhas, like images in a mirror, not a hair obscured, cause and effect manifest. In sum, all is inconceivable. At first the mind of the maker certainly did not know the mind of the destroyer, and how could the mind of the former destroyer know the mind of today’s maker? Thus the maker is the cause of the destroyer, and the destroyer the condition of the maker. If one contemplates the mind through the object, this is precisely what is meant by light intertwining, like a net of jeweled pearls, purity and defilement appearing together, good and evil both manifest, past and future of one and the same horizon. How much more, since the Buddha-realm is like space and depends on nothing; and as for the accomplishment of karmic conditions, it is like clouds rising in the long sky — how could it be conceived or discussed? Now the bhikṣu Ding, with bitter heart and exhausted thought, wishes to build a pavilion in the air and adorn a dharmakāya beyond images, to expound a wordless true sūtra and perform an inconceivable Buddhist work. It is like gazing at a wisp of cloud in a clear sky: will not the eyes stare until they ache? My thought is that sky-flowers will rise in confusion and surely fill the great limit; a drop of water becomes a cliff and surely floods the earth. Then one will see the wondrous adorned land built within a single hair, and the pure dharmakāya revealed in a single thought. It will surely make all Buddhas praise, saying, “Wondrous, wondrous! Now when I attain Buddhahood, I shall universally see all gods, men, asuras, magistrates, elders, laymen, and laywomen — the four assemblies — each within his own mind attaining equal perfect awakening and turning the great Dharma-wheel”; and it will cause all who see and hear to bring forth the mind of supreme bodhi. Those who formerly made, abided, destroyed, and emptied will all together enter the ocean of the lotus treasury. This whole expanse of vast merit and karmic cause is in truth inconceivable in every way. The ocean-seal śramaṇa, hearing this karmic cause, sighed that it had never been, and wishing to proclaim this meaning once more, spoke these verses:

All dharmas are empty, without marks, / and ultimately neither arise nor cease; / only by reason of conditions / do forming and decay differ each from each. The Buddha-body is like space; / the light of wisdom is like the full moon. / Its emptiness pervades all things; / moonlight and space are equal. / It chooses neither pure nor foul: / in every water its shadow appears. / It does not wait for a pure pool / before it shines and illumines. The minds of all living beings / are no different from the Buddha’s wisdom; / good and evil follow conditions, / and karmic courses surely differ. All Buddha-realms are born from the minds of living beings, / like flowers in the air / appearing depending on space. / No sooner formed than decaying: / they arise from space itself. / How then could today’s emptiness / fail to accomplish a surpassing work? Heaven and hell, / noble and base, all kinds of reward, / the experiences of suffering and joy — / none but are made by the mind. / One makes and oneself receives; / one adorns one’s own dharmakāya. / Straight from within marks / one ascends to the ever-abiding fruit. Excellent, O sons of the Buddha: / resolve with certainty to believe your own minds. / Each give up what you love and treasure / to adorn the Buddha’s own land. The world is all suffering, / impermanent and without self. / At birth nothing comes with one; / at death nothing goes. / Coming and going are originally empty: / why cling to them in bitterness? Meeting this great karmic cause, / why not bring forth courage? / Break once the root of stinginess and love, / and at once accomplish supreme awakening. All who have the karmic bond (text missing).
An Appeal for Building the Life-Protecting Embankment at the Three Pools

The Buddha said that filial piety is called precept: it means being filial to father and mother, filial to the Three Jewels, filial to the Dharma of the supreme Way, and filial to all living beings. If so, then one who receives the Buddha’s precepts must extend them to living beings. From of old: Master Zhiyi of Tiantai in the Sui, Vinaya Master Weixuan in the Tang, Master Yongming in the Song, and in our Ming, Master Yunqi alone. As for releasing-life ponds, apart from Shangfang and Beiyuan in the city, there is the Wan’gong Pool that he himself redeemed, and the layman Yu Deyuan with Master Dahe dredged the Three Pools of West Lake: their vast hearts were enough to save living beings as many as the sands of the Ganges. When I came to Huxin Temple I learned that three pagodas had long stood there in ruin; now they are to be rebuilt, to make for the beings saved a banner of light. Yesterday I chanced to dream of gathering sand, and the plan is already agreed. I also observed that the embankment of the Three Pools is very thin and cannot serve the released beings as a moat of gold; I fear that when the spring floods rise once, the beings already saved will drift again in the sea of suffering. Then not only would the former work be in vain, but in the end no later effect could be reaped; this is greatly to be feared. Moreover the gathering of sand cannot be reckoned by days and nights. Just as I hesitated, I chanced to come to Changming Temple and met the layman Tang Yangxing, an intimate of Yunqi. He spoke of having no son and of seeking deliverance. I rejoiced and spurred him, saying: in ancient times the Buddha had no son, and looked on the living beings of the three realms as his only son; to this day everyone calls him the Compassionate Father. Why do you not, layman, with the mind that thinks of a son, think of all living beings? Then in future the name of Compassionate Father will fill the worlds of the ten directions. For now you should think of the beings already saved in the Three Pools: if you can build a bulwark to protect them, so that the living beings within are as in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, then those before you will all call you Compassionate Father — why wait for the future? If you, layman, once raise the call, those who wish to be compassionate fathers will be many. Then the heavenly palace and Pure Land — why abandon what is before your eyes and seek elsewhere? Those who have wisdom will be moved by a thousand responses at a single hearing, without waiting for the words to finish. The old man has great hopes of you.

Preface Presented to the Venerable Wujin on His Appointment as Dharma-Excellence of the Office of Monks and Abbot of the Pure Land Chan Monastery in Pingyang (Written in Prison)

In the twenty-third year of the sage emperor’s gracious rule, because of famine in all quarters and troubles east and west, the Minister of Agriculture reported the treasury exhausted, and an edict was issued greatly opening the way of imperial favor: common people of the wilds who possessed talent or skill and wished to render some small service might, following the precedent, contribute grain and be granted office in various grades. Within or beyond the household life, even the followers of the two teachings were included. The Venerable Wujin was a son of the Yang family of Pingyang in Shanxi. In early years he was ordained at the Pure Land Monastery of the prefecture and always set his will on the one road above. He carried his umbrella through a hundred cities, visiting teachers far and wide; he trained at Niufeng and awakened at Shaoshi; he hid his traces at Zhongnan, received instruction at the Five Peaks, and formed a Dharma society of fifty-three men. He exhausted the twelve divisions of the ocean of teachings and penetrated the one mind, and completed the myriad practices. Passing through his old home, the magistrates, elders, laymen, and the four assemblies begged him to teach the Dharma, and each donated gold; following the clear precedent they contributed, and he was granted the office of Dharma-Excellence of the Office of Monks and made abbot of the Pure Land Monastery. Thus he relies on the state’s titles and vessels as a ground for protecting the Dharma, to spread the ford and bridge widely and open the road of awakening. The famous monasteries and teachers of the capital, such as the Venerable Jing’an Jie and his peers, all congratulated him on behalf of the Dharma of the region, and asked this unwise one for a piece of writing to present to him, saying: I have heard that when the Great Hero appeared in the world, his traces appeared at Kapilavastu and his Way covered the three realms. In establishing his teaching, he took pure world-transcendence as the main thing, and because of his vast perfect fusion nothing was left ungathered; hence he responded with bodies without choosing kind, benefiting beings according to place. Capacity and response meet and reflect each other, like clear water reflecting the moon, without involving thought — as with Avalokiteśvara’s universal gate and Sudhana’s universal reverence. Seen thus, is the world-transcending Dharma truly apart from the world? Therefore he does not destroy borrowed names but speaks of the true mark, the wonder lying in perfect awakening to the one mind and the sudden fusion of all dharmas: realizing suchness within conventional truth and ascending to the ultimate fruit through the myriad practices. Truly he does not count the one who sits upright in non-doing, sunk and drunk in extinction, as the attainment. Since the Dharma-line flowed east, from the Han to the present more than two thousand years, not to speak of the teaching of images spreading far: even those who cultivated in accord with the Dharma, wielding both the provisional and the actual, and made its Way manifest, were more than one. Hence the rulers of the world through the dynasties revered the teaching and honored its men, with institutions that varied; but our Sage Founder and Divine Ancestor, in founding the enterprise and handing down the succession, made laws and measures detailed and complete, encompassing the finest particulars. As their followers multiplied, they established offices to lead them: in the two capitals an Office of Monks was set up to govern the prefectures and counties, and each prefecture and county set up a Buddhist regulator and a director to lead the temples, with ranks differing. Those of excellent conduct and cultivation were selected and granted office in order, each having his charge. The reason is that they borrow the worldly Dharma to protect the Buddhadharma, precisely to realize the ultimate truth within conventional truth. Those who hold the office mostly take spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings as their ability, like the ancients who fanned the Way in a region; they surely do not take name and position as glory. Now the Venerable Wujin lifts his will above the dust and his traces beyond the world; what he has used to reveal the supreme first principle above is surely kept secret. Yet the sincerity with which the four assemblies look to him is like a bell in its frame: the sound issues outward — could that be so without substance? He must have surpassing conduct; how could he be compared to one who clings to a borrowed name and is blind to the true mark? The sūtra says that one who seeks the Dharma in sounds, forms, and marks does not see the Dharma. Therefore I say: if now these four assemblies seek bodhi in sound and form, they fail the Venerable; and if the Venerable clings to a borrowed name in teaching the Dharma, he fails the four assemblies. I have heard that one who fails his teacher falls, and one who fails the assembly is arrogant. If either is present, how can one make bright the Buddha-sun and repay the court’s grace in protecting the Dharma? The Venerable is going. If your road passes through the golden world, put the words of this sick old man of Vaiśālī to Mañjuśrī’s chamber, and proclaim them to the great assembly: may each, by means of the borrowed name, realize the true mark, and by this ford and bridge leap at once to the other shore. When the bhikṣus heard these words, they bowed and departed.
Preface Seeing Off the Venerable Jian on His Journey to Bagui

The Venerable has been a monk for many years. At first, because he came to the old man in study, he brought forth the mind of supreme bodhi. Lately, with his fellow practitioners, he invited Mr. Ou Boyu and together they formed the Udumbara Society beneath the bodhi tree, borrowing its shade and daily enjoying the coolness of its joy. Each half month they asked the old man to sit beneath the tree on the bodhi seat and wave the whisk, expounding for the assembly the Dharma-practice of cultivating and advancing in supreme bodhi. From spring to summer, four months have already passed. The Venerable bowed and said he would go to Bagui to visit an old friend amid green hills and white clouds; and since he would be wandering from place to place, saving beings as conditions arise, he wished to cause all who hear and all who see to bring forth the mind of supreme bodhi, as the first step of the ford and bridge out of the world. The old man rejoiced and said to him: Excellent, son of the Buddha. You should know that all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, in whatever they do, ever make one thing their work — namely, teaching living beings by this bodhi-mind; hence it is one great matter. Whether going forth into birth or entering death, it is by this cause, by this condition; apart from this one thing there is no other. Though the body pass through perilous roads and experience all the three evil paths, if one can cause even a single person to bring forth the bodhi-mind, one is willing to bear every suffering. Therefore the sages’ conduct is not in vain; their works are all real, because in the worldly and the world-transcending there is not one dharma beyond this bodhi-mind, this bodhi-practice, this bodhi-work. What is called bodhi is a Sanskrit word meaning awakening. Awakening is the Buddha-nature that all living beings originally possess: numinous knowing, still and illumining, hence true awakening; clearly awakening of oneself, hence solitary awakening; brightly and greatly penetrating, shattering the heavy darkness, hence great awakening. Using it daily without knowing it is called non-awakening. Non-awakening makes one an ordinary person, and the ordinary person is a living being. Because living beings each possess this numinous awakened nature yet use it daily without knowing it — alas, to possess it and not know it, is that not pitiable? Not knowing, one cannot use it; not using it, one is like one who holds a pearl yet begs, who carries a treasure and loses his way, suffering hardship in vain, driven through birth and death, willingly falling into the sea of suffering. Is that not pitiable? Therefore the sages do not grieve over what is not to be grieved but grieve over what is; hence they appear in the world and open and guide by all kinds of skillful means. This is what is meant by awakening oneself and being able to awaken others, the already awakened awakening the yet unawakened. Now one who awakens himself is not deluded about things; one who awakens others does not abandon things. Not being deluded, one gathers things into oneself; not abandoning, one gives oneself to follow others. Because one gathers them into oneself, one does not see that there are things; because one follows others, one does not see that there is a self. Not having things, all things are wondrous; not having a self, the self is not real. Knowing the self is not real, the self is the things; knowing all things are wondrous, the things are the real. When the things are the real, things are not things; and the self is not the self. Things and self both not, going and coming without marks, the myriad conditions silently still, one Way empty and at leisure — this is the mind-doctrine of the Great Awakened One and the wondrous practice of all bodhisattvas. Thus the two awakenings are complete and the two benefits fulfilled: this is what is meant by manifesting all deportments through the practice of extinction, benefiting others according to circumstance as the wondrous practice of bodhi. Otherwise, to be driven along perilous roads, to wade mountains and rivers, to weary sinew and bone and afflict the body, to increase burning affliction, to diminish good roots, and to lengthen the evil destinies — that is not the work of accomplishing bodhi and teaching living beings. The Venerable is going. Going upstream, the grey cloud-mountains — all before your eyes are true realms; the crying of apes and the call of cranes — all in your ears are true sūtras; the Zhuang and Yao peoples and the orangutans — all you meet are true Buddhas; flowing water and moving wind — all are the broad and long tongue; blue sky and white moon — all are the pure body. Awakening thus, every place is a bodhi court, every step a land of ultimate bliss, every thought true cultivation, every matter true practice. What then is there to reckon of the world-transcending and the worldly, of self-benefit and other-benefit? Can the Venerable believe and receive the old man’s words? If you have any doubt, on your way through Mount Xiang, put it to the Buddha of Measureless Life.
